articles.title_orig: What the US midterms mean for ties with China
articles.title_zh: What the US midterms mean for ties with China
articles.content_orig:
The US election results could embolden Congress to exert greater control over trade policy, though president retains broad sway, analysts say
The Democrats’ comprehensive victory in the US midterm elections could embolden Congress to assert greater authority over trade policy and scrutinise the deals President Donald Trump made with China, analysts say, though a dramatic shift in Washington’s trade policy is unlikely.
“Congress, including pro-free trade Republicans who have been intimidated into standing down, might be inclined to reassert some degree of congressional authority on trade,” said Stephen Olson, a former US trade negotiator.
As Trump retained broad executive discretion over tariffs, a major shift in trade policy was improbable, added Olson, who is also a visiting senior fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.

articles.title_orig: Datacenters were on the ballot. US voters rejected them
articles.title_zh: Datacenters were on the ballot. US voters rejected them
articles.content_orig:
Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total in Tuesday’s elections
Track live results from all 50 states
Send us your questions about the US midterms results and Democrats’ ‘blue wave’
There were three big losers in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US: Donald Trump, Elon Musk and datacenters.
Datacenters, the facilities full of semiconductor chips that power artificial intelligence and a host of other online products, were on the ballot in elections in at least 40 jurisdictions across 10 states. Voters responded with a strong rebuke of the giant buildings, which have has become a symbol of the tech industry and AI.
In Ohio alone, at least 14 municipalities passed bans or restrictions on datacenter development, including in Sunbury, where Amazon has proposed a $2m datacenter project. In Maine, eight municipalities passed temporary datacenter moratoriums. In Emporio, Kansas, where a 1,000-acre gigawatt-scale datacenter was recently proposed, a ban on high-impact datacenters was approved by voters.
Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total, with one notable exception: Hardwood, North Dakota. The small city of a population of less than 1,000 people voted down a bill that would impose restrictions on datacenter development.
Where datacenters were not explicitly on the ballot, officials who have pushed back against their development were elected. In Texas , Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who secured a historical victory as governor on Tuesday night over her Republican opponent, has promised to impose moratoriums on their construction. She has pledged to implement greater restrictions on and community input into whether datacenters can be built. Towards the end of his tenure, Greg Abbott, her Republican opponent, had also tried to capitalize on anti-datacenter sentiment, demanding an end to electricity subsidies for them. He reversed his previous stance that had welcomed datacenters to the state.
Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became governor of Georgia, and Amy Acton, the newly elected governor of Ohio , have also pledged to implement moratoria on the construction of large datacenters.
Anti-datacenter sentiment has grown in the last few months has become a bipartisan issue. In May, Florida governor Ron DeSantis signed a bill imposing strict regulations on large-scale datacenters. Still, last night’s election solidified the overwhelming opposition to these centers of compute that have come to serve as a stand-in for the ultra wealthy and resource extraction by the AI industry.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Elon Musk, who poured over $400m into supporting conservative candidates, posted on X.
Analyst Dan Ives said the results of the midterms are a clear sign that the pace of datacenter buildout will start to slow down.
after newsletter promotion
“There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next two years,” Ives said. Ives said he was particularly worried about Hinojosa who is a “known anti-datacenter politician”.
“The biggest worry of the night for tech investors and the AI trade was around the state of Texas where 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Jumps 1,500 Points On Democratic Sweep of Congress — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Jumps 1,500 Points On Democratic Sweep of Congress — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared nearly 1,600 points, or 3%, on Wednesday, its biggest gain of the year, as investors digested the impact of the Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm congressional elections.
Other indexes also jumped, with the broader S&P 500 climbing 120 points, or 1.6%, to close at 7,689 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index gaining 1.4%.
"Investors are happy to have the midterms out of the way," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told investors in a report. "This was a major source of uncertainty, and putting it in the rear-view mirror removes a key obstacle heading into a very favorable time of year seasonally."
The shifting political winds could affect a range of issues that influence investment returns, from the pace of the data center buildout and cryptocurrency industry regulation to proposals to cap credit card interest rates.
At the same time, Wall Street analysts do not expect the outcome to derail a stock market being driven more by robust corporate profits and solid economic growth than by politics.
"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said in a note to investors.
Stocks of solar power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans.
Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Mr. Trump's social media company, the artificial intelligence sector and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Trump Media & Technology's stock price fell nearly 25% on Wednesday, while shares of Musk-owned SpaceX and Tesla sank 3.8% and 3.3%, respectively.
Investors also expect the election results to heighten gridlock in Congress, with Democratic lawmakers now in control of both the House and Senate, and Mr. Trump threatening to wield his veto power to block any legislation he opposes.
Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to Wall Street analysts.
Meanwhile, stocks have generally performed well following midterm elections. The S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 15.5% in the six months after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970, according to figures from investment firm Edward Jones.
"Economic growth, inflation, interest rates and corporate earnings have historically mattered more to broad investment performance than the party composition of Congress, especially if the president and congressional leadership come from different parties," analysts with the Wells Fargo Investment Institute said in a report.
"We do not expect sweeping policy changes," they added. "More likely, in our view, is a split-government alignment on affordability, energy policy and opportunities from artificial intelligence."
Beyond the Beltway, the midterm electoral results could affect key issues for investors, such as the pace of data center construction, with enormous spending on artificial intelligence helping drive stocks to record highs this year while also raising concerns about a bubble in tech stocks .
"In divided government, the policy implications at the federal level may be limited, but data center policy decisions sit at the state and utility-commission level, making gubernatorial and utility races important alongside Congress, particularly Governor Abbott's loss in Texas," Jeff Buchbinder of LPL Research told investors.
"LPL Research continues to expect the buildout to occur, but strong performances by Democrats in key data center states (and pushback from the 'not in my backyard' folks) may slow it down some, potentially increasing regulatory pressure on AI infrastructure stocks including semiconductors, machinery and power generation," he added.

articles.title_orig: China, US defence officials agree to improve ‘communication’ to reduce risks
articles.title_zh: China, US defence officials agree to improve ‘communication’ to reduce risks
articles.content_orig:
Military officials from two countries to work on promoting ‘effective’ crisis management after constructive meeting in Washington
US and Chinese defence officials met in Washington for the first meeting of a Crisis Communications and Prevention Working Group established under an agreement announced in September when leaders of the two nations met.
The two sides agreed on the importance of “advancing practical communication measures” to reduce risks between the US and China, according to a Pentagon readout of the meeting released Tuesday. Delegates also discussed “additional channels” to promote “effective” crisis management and ways to communicate “expediently and effectively”.

articles.title_orig: Canada, China Extend Tariff Deal, Aim to Boost Canadian Exports
articles.title_zh: Canada, China Extend Tariff Deal, Aim to Boost Canadian Exports
articles.content_orig:
The federal government announced on Wednesday that China will extend its soon-to-expire tariff-free treatment for some Canadian agricultural and seafood products for another two years.
After Prime Minister Mark Carney's January trip to Beijing, China struck a deal with Ottawa that saw it pause its 100 per cent tariffs on Canadian canola meal and peas, and 25 per cent tariffs on lobster and crab.
That deal, which took effect in March, promised to keep tariffs off those products only until the end of 2026.
"This extension gives farmers, producers and harvesters predictable access to the Chinese market, and it's how we will grow our exports to China by 50 per cent by 2030," International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said in a statement.
Canada reaches tariff-quota deal with China on EVs, canola
Canadian canola has seen some tough years. This could be one of its best
During that January trip, Carney also got Beijing to cut tariffs on canola seed imports from 100 per cent to about 15 per cent for a period of five years.
Canada is the top global exporter of canola and China is the industry's second-largest market after the U.S.
When he signed that initial agreement, Carney made concessions of his own, agreeing to allow up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles per year into the Canadian market with a tariff rate of 6.1 per cent.
'Great relief' in Canada's fishing sector as China lifts lobster and crab tariffs: minister
That brought the tariff on Chinese-made EVs down from the 100 per cent level set by the Trudeau government in 2024. China had hiked its tariffs on Canadian goods in response.
The January deal also saw Canada grant improved market access for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products that are in short supply in Canada and cannot be made by Canadian producers.
The federal government announced on Wednesday that it will also extend its market access for those steel and aluminum products until the end of 2028.
Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s election commission rejects Netanyahu claims of voting fraud
articles.title_zh: Israel’s election commission rejects Netanyahu claims of voting fraud
articles.content_orig:
Move comes after attorney general blocks Shin Bet call to interrogate politicians from Palestinian-led parties
Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of last week’s vote that stripped Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition of its governing majority, rejecting claims of mass fraud promoted by the prime minister.
The main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, said Netanyahu had launched a “pogrom against democracy” in attempting to hold on to power by discrediting valid votes and weaponising security forces against parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel .
Hours earlier, Israel’s attorney general said she had blocked a demand from the Shin Bet security service to interrogate senior politicians from the Palestinian-led parties because she had not been presented with any evidence of wrongdoing.
“In a country governed by the rule of law, neither citizens nor elected officials can be interrogated without evidence that justifies doing so,” Gali Baharav-Miara said in a statement, after Haaretz reported on the attempt to target four politicians.
Election authorities on Wednesday presented the final results to the president, Isaac Herzog, after rejecting allegations they had been tainted by large-scale foreign interference and voter fraud.
“The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the Central Elections Committee said in a statement.
The body’s chair, Noam Sohlberg, said some “suspicions” were still under investigation but “they do not cast doubt on the election as a whole or justify delaying the election results”.
When the results were handed over, Herzog denounced racist attacks on Palestinian citizens who had turned out to vote at historic rates.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said. “I hold Arab society in Israel in great respect. I value its contribution to the country in every area of life, and its desire to integrate.”
Herzog will play a key role in the formation of the next government by choosing which politician has the first chance to create a coalition. He is expected to name Eisenkot, and the announcement could come as early as Thursday evening.
Late on Wednesday, the Palestinian grouping Ra’am said it would recommend that Eisenkot form the next government. The larger Palestinian grouping, Joint List, has said its priority is removing Netanyahu, so is expected to back Eisenkot as the strongest contender to achieve that.
A former leader of the Israeli military who lost his son fighting in Gaza, Eisenkot has secured the public support of all of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties.
However, negotiations could take weeks and Eisenkot warned of ongoing attempts to undermine trust in the election results. He accused Netanyahu of weaponising the security services against domestic opponents in an effort to hold on to power.
“The employees of the Ministry of Defense, law enforcement and the civil service in Israel are servants of the state, not the king,” he said in a statement. “Woe to anyone who abuses their authority and role for political considerations.”
The Shin Bet chief, David Zini, handpicked for the role by Netanyahu, had ordered the interrogations and sought to classify the investigation as a security file, which would have allowed harsher conditions including barring the politicians from having legal counsel.
Nadav Eyal, an Israeli journalist and commentator, said the public should brace for more extreme attempts to dismiss election results and discredit the leading opposition parties.
“The groundwork is steadily being laid for violence,” he wrote on X. “What you’re hearing breaking right now is the foundation of the legal and governmental orders in Israel.”
Netanyahu presided over a racist campaign targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel – about 20% of the population – and on election day began promoting the unfounded accusations of mass fraud now rejected by election authorities.
Ahmad Tibi, one of the most prominent and effective Palestinian politicians, was reportedly among those the Shin Bet sought to interrogate. He responded to the latest allegations, as news broke of sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterms, with a swipe at Netanyahu’s fear of democracy.
“[The] attorney general is checking suspicion of ties between the Joint List and Democrats in the US,” Tibi wrote in a social media post. “According to the suspicion, in both cases the same sophisticated method was employed: people arrived in droves at the polling stations, cast a slip, and went home.”

articles.title_orig: Rumor: Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds datamine leaks Year 2 characters
articles.title_zh: Rumor: Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds datamine leaks Year 2 characters
articles.content_orig:
Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds may have been hit with a new leak, revealing potential characters coming to the game in Year 2.
As many of you know, SEGA released a massive 2.0.0 update last week. Unsurprisingly, it didn’t take fans long to get to work and datamine the new files. It’s through this apparent datamine shared by VocaloidMikuBr that we may have an idea about which characters are coming in the future.
First, let’s talk about the Final Fantasy 7 Remake DLC. According to the game’s files, Cloud Strife and Tifa Lockhart have entries in the files. To be fair, these aren’t surprising picks – they’re two of the most popular characters from Final Fantasy 7. However, perhaps someone would have expected Sephiroth to make it into the racer over Tifa.
For free characters, there’s someone called “Marisa” in the files. Some are speculating that this could be a Touhou collaboration, but that remains to be seen.
A number of other characters have been spotted as well. These include Movie Sonic, Will (potentially from Metaphor: ReFantazio), Sakura Shinguji from Sakura Wars, and Akira Yuki from Virtua Fighter.
Keep in mind that this datamine isn’t a full reveal of everything SEGA has planned for the game. Also, as nothing has been announced, these characters are not officially confirmed just yet.
In case you missed it, we have the huge patch notes for the Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds 2.0.0 update . The game is available on Nintendo Switch 2 and Switch.
Do any of these characters interest you? Share your thoughts with us in the comments below.

articles.title_orig: 7 worst midterm predictions
articles.title_zh: 7 worst midterm predictions
articles.content_orig:
If you looked at the polling , the ad spending , the campaign messaging , the early-vote turnout , and historic midterm trends, you had a feeling Tuesday would be a good night for Democrats.
All metrics pointed to the fact that voters wanted to punish President Donald Trump over his tariffs and war in Iran. And because the only way for Americans to do that was to vote against Trump’s party, Republicans ended the night by losing at least seven Senate seats and dozens of seats in the House.
Yet Republicans, believing they would overperform polling as they had in 2016, 2020, and 2024, deluded themselves into believing all was well. In fact, a number were so confident they made wild predictions that the party would hold on to their congressional majorities.
The predictions were absurd before the election but are even more hilarious to look at now.
Here are seven awful predictions of the cycle:
Johnson made this prediction on Oct. 29 in an appearance on Fox News:
“Hakeem Jeffries will not have a race for speaker, because Republicans are going to win. I’ll be the speaker in the next Congress. I’ll be administering the oath to some of these people who ran for Congress as Marxists, sadly. We’ll see what happens, but he’s going to have to run. Hakeem wants to remain the leader of the Democrats. He’ll be the minority leader if he wins, but they’re going to hold him hostage for all sorts of things. This is a taste of what’s to come. It’s a harbinger of what’s to come for the Democrat Party.”
Mike Johnson: "Republicans are gonna win. I'll be the Speaker in the next Congress." (Bookmark this) (Also, stay for Ainsley Earhardt's comment at the end of the clip 😆) pic.twitter.com/jNIk9R0ojZ
Turns out, Johnson will not be swearing any members in—and he won’t even have a leadership role in the next Congress.
The Daily Mail published a barn burner of an article about the chaos at the White House on Election Day. Nestled in the piece is this gem about what Wiles and LaCivita had been telling Trump in the lead up to Election Day:
As recently as September, the source said, Wiles was telling people directly that Republicans were going to take the midterms.
The source also described weekly Thursday briefings at which veteran GOP political consultant Chris LaCivita, a key Wiles ally, would promise the President that the win was his.
On Tuesday morning, staffers in the West Wing were still talking about picking up seats in both chambers.
‘Delusional,’ the source said. ‘They were delusional right until the very end.’
Blair was one of the masterminds behind Republicans’ efforts to gerrymander their way to a House majority. And after the gerrymandering wars ended, he wrote this in May in a post on X: “Two weeks ago people were dooming and asking wAs rEdIsTrIcTiNg wOrTh iT? …16 net seat swing to GOP…”
Well, as of press time, it appears that only one Democratic-held district that Blair helped target with mid-decade redraws flipped.
In fact, the gerrymander North Carolina passed seems to be a dummymander, with Democrats winning more seats in the state than they had under the old map.
After Tuesday’s elections, House Democrats mocked Blair’s old tweet.
Dems have near them a poster board with a James Blair tweet—the architect of the GOP redistricting push that appears to have backfired pic.twitter.com/UDH61bRFWJ
“53 & 219,” Martin wrote in a post on X, referring to Republicans winning 53 Senate seats and 219 in the House. “Take it to the bank.”
Wonder how much he lost on that bet!
“Texas is turning blue like I’m losing my seat,” Miller texted New York Times reporter Annie Karni in July, when she asked him about the state of his race after being accused of domestic violence .
“You’re better than this,” he added.
Well, Miller lost , and Texas turned blue up and down the ballot.
“For all the panicans…. It’s a red sweep in the senate I’m convinced,” Santos, the disgraced former Republican congressman, wrote just after 10 AM ET on Election Day.
He also made this promise: “If Ohio goes Blue for the Gov and Senator race I’m dressing in drag and doing a cold plunge! Bookmark this!”
Guess we’re getting a show.
Any media outlets using betting sites to influence their election forecasts should be named and shamed.
Bettors on morally bankrupt sites like Polymarket, where you can place bets on sick things like military strikes in Iran, do not know anything besides the vibes they get from reading the news and social media. For example, Kalshi bettors did not predict the races correctly . And they probably lost a boatload of money, too.

articles.title_orig: Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
articles.title_zh: Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
articles.content_orig:
Conservation officers say more than one bear may have been involved in attack on women near their home
Search teams in Canada have discovered the body of a 20-year-old woman and confirmed that both she and her mother were killed in an attack that conservation officers now believe could have involved multiple grizzly bears.
Late on Tuesday, conservation officers in British Columbia said the two women, who were reported missing over the weekend, were located near a trail a short distance from their home.
The discovery has shaken a community where, earlier in the year, a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and their teachers.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre of the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said in a video posted online. Tyre later said the conservation service was investigating the possibility that more than one bear was involved in the fatal attack.
“We appreciate people’s concerns and the desire to assist but it is critical the public stay out of the area – both due to the danger and to allow officers to do their work,” he said.
Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter Selah Reed were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Balcarras’s remains were found first and Reed was located a day later.
A fundraiser for Balcarras started by her family mourned a woman who had recently moved to Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, for a new job and “to start a new chapter” of her life. She leaves behind three adult children and a grandchild.
“[Jenny] was working toward building a future and had not yet had the opportunity to establish savings or put aside funds to help her family with unexpected expenses such as these,” wrote relative Mary Melissa Smith. “Tragically, no one could have anticipated that her family would be faced with such an unimaginable loss.”
The family also mourned 20-year-old Selah, who had her “whole life ahead of her” before the attack.
“She was only beginning her journey into adulthood, making this loss even more heartbreaking,” wrote Smith.
Both Balcarras and Reed had lived in communities in remote and rugged parts of the province, as well as time in Alaska.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (5 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.
Bella Coola, which sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast, is a remote location, and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.
Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.
Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said on Tuesday: “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.” Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.
The province’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, called the news “heartbreaking” and said he was thinking of the victims’ family and the Nuxalk Nation.
“At a time of such profound grief and uncertainty, my thoughts are with everyone who is hurting and with all those supporting one another through an incredibly difficult day.”

articles.title_orig: What Wall Street billionaires are saying about Democrats' midterm sweep
articles.title_zh: What Wall Street billionaires are saying about Democrats' midterm sweep
articles.content_orig:
America's billionaires woke up Wednesday to a political reckoning — and a Wall Street rally.
As Democrats celebrated a sweeping midterm victory , some of the country's wealthiest donors traded barbs over record election spending . Others warned the results could threaten the artificial intelligence boom.
Wall Street, however, cheered the outcome. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4%, as investors welcomed political gridlock , reduced uncertainty and President Donald Trump's willingness to accept the results.
Virgin Group founder Richard Branson took aim at the billions spent influencing the election.
"I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent," Branson wrote Wednesday on LinkedIn , calling for campaign finance reform. Branson did not give donations that met the threshold reporting in the 2026 election cycle.
His comments came as Elon Musk, the election's largest individual donor , watched his preferred Republicans lose the Texas Senate and governor races despite pouring $224 million into the state — nearly half his record $474 million in political giving nationwide, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records.
Early Wednesday, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO suggested on X that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing before joking that his "election-interfering space lasers" had failed.
LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman , another major political donor, took a sharper tone.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote late Tuesday on X , accusing Musk of spending "outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power" while defending his own contributions to Democrats.
Other Democratic megadonors celebrated. "The world changed yesterday," Alex Soros wrote Wednesday on X, hailing the results as a generational victory after his family contributed roughly $103 million to Democratic political efforts.
But beyond the political sparring, some of the country's richest investors were focused on a potentially bigger consequence of the Democratic sweep : the future of the AI boom .
Even before polls closed Tuesday, Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman warned on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that slowing AI development could jeopardize America's technological edge. "Practically speaking, we can't slow down," he said.
As results rolled in Tuesday night, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya sounded an even starker warning.
Palihapitiya initially questioned whether the early results would hold, but warned that if they did, the implications for the AI trade could be severe.
"And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers," Palihapitiya said during an election-night livestream of the "All-In" podcast.
Texas offered an early test of those fears. Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has proposed a moratorium on new data-center construction until stronger safeguards are established, defeated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.
During the same livestream, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner warned the Democratic wave could mean at least 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI data-center capacity would not come online in 2027. Wall Street analyst Dan Ives estimated Wednesday that 10% of planned U.S. data centers would no longer go ahead.
AMD CEO Lisa Su acknowledged the growing resistance to AI's expansion , urging technology companies to demonstrate the benefits of data centers to local communities.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," Su told CNBC Wednesday .
Yet Wall Street may have found opportunity in the same slowdown that worried AI's biggest backers.
Fewer new data centers could increase the value of existing facilities while easing the enormous spending burden on technology giants. Big Tech stocks surged Wednesday , adding more than $750 billion in market value at one point, even as smaller, debt-dependent data-center operators tumbled.

Democratic victories and opposition to AI infrastructure highlight concerns over power bills, water use and the impact on local communities
Strong voter backlash in the US midterm elections against AI infrastructure projects, including data centres, indicates that framing the domestic buildout as key to competing with China failed to convince Americans and underscores the need to address local concerns, according to analysts.
“The argument that we need to build more data centres to win in AI against China no longer seems to have the kind of resonance it did before, if it ever did, frankly,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Centre.
Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, echoed that assessment, saying: “The lesson is that invoking China as a justification for tech and industrial investment is becoming less effective.”

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing
articles.content_orig:
A bodycam video has been released by Ukraine police which they say shows the moments between two powerful Russian bomb strikes that killed at least 40 people at an aid centre and a shelter.
The footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, shows residents of the southern village of Kamyshuvakha going to an underground shelter after the first attack on Monday. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said more than 30 people may still be under the rubble, as a search operation continued for the third day.
Nine gliding bombs, some weighing 3,000kg, hit the village as people had gathered to get humanitarian aid, Ukraine said.
The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.
It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, as shocked local residents stare at the rubble.
Severely damaged buildings are also seen.
A voice of a military official is then heard on a two-way radio warning police on the ground of more glide bombs being launched towards Kamyshuvakha.
"Quickly [go] to the shelter!" one of the police officers tells local residents, who are seen walking into the shelter - at least two floors underground.
Seconds later the shelter is hit, and the recording stops.
Ukraine said the shelter was near a local school, which was being used to distribute humanitarian aid.
BBC Verify has confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage released by the Ukrainian state emergencies service DSNS showing the aftermath Monday's attack in Komyshuvakha.
In a post on social media on Wednesday, Zelensky said that "nine aerial bombs were dropped by the Russians.
"First, they hit people who came to receive humanitarian aid, and then rescuers and police officers who arrived at the scene."
The Ukrainian president added that "unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack", describing it as yet another of "thousands" of war crimes committed by Russia.
Ukraine's DSNS earlier posted another video showing a huge crater left after the attack on Kamyshuvakha.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
In a separate development on Wednesday, Zelensky said he talked "in great detail for an hour-and-a-half" with US President Donald Trump's peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of trilateral negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the US on 10-11 November in Abu-Dhabi.
The Ukrainian leader - who is currently making a surprise visit to Spain - also said his team had a separate "meaningful" meeting in Brussels with representatives from the US, the EU, France, Britain, Germany, as well as Nato and the World Bank about "post-war reconstruction".
He added that the meeting in Belgium's capital would continue on Thursday to discuss "security guarantees" for Ukraine.
Since the trilateral talks aimed at ending the war were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
Analysts expect no major breakthrough when the talks resume in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.
Additional reporting Paul Brown, BBC Verify

articles.title_orig: Nintendo’s biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business
articles.title_zh: Nintendo’s biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business
articles.content_orig:
For years, the AI industry’s insatiable demand for memory and storage has had plenty of knock-on effects on the price and availability of PC components like RAM , SSDs , and GPUs . Now those shortages are also squeezing the supply of ROM chips that power physical Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 game cartridges.
Chip manufacturer Macronix announced in its third-quarter earnings report that the company’s production of ROM chips “has reached its end” and that it will begin “gradually decoupling from the game industry,” as reported by Taiwanese news site BigGo Finance . That could be an issue for Nintendo, which analyst David Gibson notes uses Macronix as its “main memory chip maker” for physical game cartridges.
That ROM production—which has shrunk 39 percent in the last year and now represents just 5 percent of Macronix’s business—is being crowded out by production of more lucrative, in-demand chips like NOR- and NAND-based memory and eMMCs, the company said. With Macronix’s production capacity stuck at 25,000 12-inch wafers a month—and $1.2 billion in planned new capacity taking a year or more to spin up—less profitable ROM chips are taking up wafer space that can earn more through other types of chips.
This doesn’t mean Nintendo will follow Sony into a world without physical game production . On the contrary, the Switch maker said last month that it had no plans to give up on the game cartridges in the near future. But those cartridges could get more expensive to produce as Nintendo is forced to rely on suppliers like Rohm and Lapis Semiconductor for its remaining ROM chips.
That could have a knock-on effect on the prices publishers charge for physical Switch cartridges, too. Earlier this year, Nintendo started charging more for some physical games than for the equivalent digital download. And last year , Japanese publisher Inin only committed to a full Switch cartridge release for R-Type Dimensions III after it said “two new smaller cartridge [storage capacity] sizes for Nintendo Switch 2” lowered the cost of producing those carts.
On the other hand, Gibson notes that digital software sales represented 61.5 percent of Nintendo’s business in the second calendar quarter of 2026, up slightly from the year before. If that number keeps increasing, lower demand for ROM-based Nintendo cartridges could end up balancing out the costs involved in due time.

articles.title_orig: Trump Media’s Shares Fall to Record Low After Midterms
articles.title_zh: Trump Media’s Shares Fall to Record Low After Midterms
articles.content_orig:
President Trump’s social media company recorded one of its biggest daily market losses on Wednesday, a day after Democrats scored staggering victories in the midterm elections.
Shares of Trump Media & Technology Group plunged 24 percent to close at $4.49 — a low for the parent company of Truth Social.
On Wall Street, trading in shares of Trump Media have always been something of a proxy for Mr. Trump’s popularity. But the decline in Trump Media’s stock price has accelerated in recent months as its quarterly losses have mounted.
With the most recent sell-off, shares of Trump Media are down more than 90 percent from the closing price on the stock’s first day of trading , on March 26, 2024. Shortly after the company made its Wall Street debut, Mr. Trump’s stake in Trump Media was valued at around $6 billion. Now it is worth just over $500 million.
And there is a fresh concern for the company: newly empowered congressional Democrats with the ability to start investigations into business dealings involving Mr. Trump and his family.
One that could face scrutiny is Trump Media’s business of selling early access to Mr. Trump’s Truth Social posts to investment firms seeking to use the information to make lightning-fast trades. Immediately after Trump Media announced plans to offer this early access to the president’s posts, several congressional Democrats denounced it as giving an unfair advantage to some traders. Other Democratic lawmakers introduced a bill that would bar Trump Media from selling this early access.

articles.title_orig: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
articles.title_zh: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
articles.content_orig:
Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday.
The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data.
One of the impersonated sites was america250.org, belonging to a non-partisan group of lawmakers, business executives, and at least one former member of the Trump administration. The attackers registered america250[.]holiday and used it as a reverse proxy to america250.org. The imposter website delivered content from the real one that added malicious JavaScript into it.
“We assess that the intrusion set may have deliberately selected this website due to its association with a high-profile national celebration, potentially leveraging the event as a pretext for invitation-themed spear-phishing campaigns,” researchers from security firm Sekoia said .
A second website, theowo[.]club, proxied the website Raffles of London OWO, a luxury hotel physically close to some of the UK’s most sensitive government institutions, including the Ministry of Defence and 10 Downing Street, the official residence and office of the British Prime Minister. Open source reporting indicates that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stayed there during a visit on October 14.
“By doing this watering hole [impersonating] the Raffles London at The OWO, the intrusion set may have sought to target diplomatic delegations and high-profile guests through targeted spear-phishing campaigns,” the researchers said.
The attackers also delivered their attacks through compromised websites—including a top Ukrainian gas production company—and a Ukrainian web analytics service that serves thousands of websites. Sekoia said its attribution to the Kremlin is based on the targets’ profiles and similarities to a previous attack attributed to APT29, one of the names the suspected Russian group is tracked under.
The hackers relied on three infection vectors: direct JavaScript injection into traffic from legitimate websites, proxy domains such as america250[.]holiday, and the supply-chain compromise of the Ukrainian web analytics service. In each case, the injected JavaScript was the same. During the first stage, the JavaScript profiled the visitor’s browser and device. The attackers then used that information to deliver one of three zero-click exploit chains, which work without requiring any interaction from the target.
One of the chains was DarkSword, an iOS exploit kit that Google researchers said customers of PARS Defense, a commercial surveillance vendor in Turkey, and at least two other threat actors have used. Sekoia said the more recent campaign used two other exploit chains that weren’t named.
All of the vulnerabilities exploited in the campaign were “n-days,” meaning they had already been patched and attacks worked only on outdated versions of iOS or Android.

articles.title_orig: NATO’s New Defense Plan Includes Strikes Deep Into Russia
articles.title_zh: NATO’s New Defense Plan Includes Strikes Deep Into Russia
articles.content_orig:
In brief: NATO is developing plans to strike targets deep inside Russia in response to an invasion of alliance territory, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday. The approach aims to halt an initial assault and disrupt Moscow’s ability to sustain further operations, though analysts question whether European leaders would authorize such strikes.
NATO is developing defense plans that envision strikes deep inside Russia if Moscow attacks alliance territory, targeting the bases, supply networks, and industrial facilities supporting an invasion.
The approach, developed under NATO’s supreme allied commander in Europe, U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, reflects lessons from Russia’s war against Ukraine: Stopping advancing troops requires disrupting the military system behind them, according to The Wall Street Journal .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
For decades, European defense planning focused on preventing Soviet or Russian forces from advancing after crossing NATO borders. Alliance strategists now consider that approach insufficient.
Polish Maj. Gen. Ireneusz Nowak told the Journal that defense also requires the ability to strike back.
In the event of a conflict with Russia, we would certainly want to strike its military-industrial base, he said, describing precision strikes deep inside Russian territory as a means of deterrence.
Nowak argued that if Ukraine had possessed that capability at the outset of the invasion, the war would not have developed into positional fighting resembling World War I.
The plans envision attacks roughly 150 kilometers (93 miles) to thousands of kilometers behind the front line, using precision missiles and less expensive weapons such as drones, the Journal reported.
Potential targets extend beyond airfields and military bases to industrial facilities, critical infrastructure, and raw material resources supporting Russia’s war effort. The aim is to make such strikes an automatic component of NATO’s response to a Russian attack.
Grynkewich outlined the approach at a recent security conference in Warsaw as part of what he called his “theory of victory.”
NATO forces would first stop the opening wave of an attack, then undermine the enemy’s ability to sustain subsequent operations. If the offensive continued, the alliance would strike both attacking forces and the networks supplying, supporting, and directing them.
The strategy does not envision escalation to nuclear weapons. NATO also held its first symposium devoted to deep strikes in June.
Precision weapons are central to the approach, including established systems such as Tomahawk cruise missiles and ATACMS ballistic missiles, alongside weapons still under development.
European countries are seeking to expand stocks of Storm Shadow, SCALP, and Taurus cruise missiles while developing additional systems.
Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defense Studies, told the newspaper that 20 European manufacturers were pursuing at least 48 projects to develop inexpensive cruise missiles, though not all would succeed.
Ukraine has increasingly pursued a similar approach, striking military and economic targets inside Russia with longer-range weapons, including domestically developed Flamingo cruise missiles, according to the report.
Analysts cautioned that military planning alone would not guarantee political approval to carry out the strikes.
Nico Lange, a former senior German Defense Ministry official, told the Journal that a gap remained between military plans incorporating offensive action to defend against Russia and political views that equate defense primarily with barriers or a “drone wall.”
The unresolved question, according to the report, is whether European leaders would authorize the operations their military planners consider necessary to stop and defeat an attack.

articles.title_orig: Zelensky doubts Musk ‘acted alone’ in Ukraine Starlink slowdown
articles.title_zh: Zelensky doubts Musk ‘acted alone’ in Ukraine Starlink slowdown
articles.content_orig:
In brief: President Volodymyr Zelensky said Elon Musk had communicated with both him and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. He did not specify when the contacts took place or what they concerned. His remarks came amid renewed scrutiny of Musk’s role in Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield, following service restrictions that disrupted some Ukrainian military operations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Elon Musk had been in communication with both him and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, in a PBS NewsHour interview aired Monday, Nov. 2.
“At the very beginning of the war, Elon had communication with Putin and with me,” Zelensky said. He gave no details about when the contacts took place, what they concerned or whether they were direct conversations.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Zelensky made the remark while discussing Ukraine’s reliance on Starlink and Starshield, satellite services operated by Musk’s SpaceX.
Asked whether he believed Musk supported Ukraine and wanted it to win, Zelensky said he did not know. He said he remained grateful for Starlink’s role during the war, but added that some of Musk’s earlier public signals about Ukraine had not seemed “pro-Ukrainian.”
One such signal came on Oct. 15, when Musk called for Zelensky to go as Kyiv raised concerns about US restrictions on satellite services and intelligence sharing.
Zelensky said he had wanted to speak with Musk after SpaceX restricted Starlink service in October, but the company did not connect them. He said he could not identify who authorized the restrictions and was unsure whether Musk could independently limit Starshield, which he described as a government version of the system.
Zelensky’s comment came days after Putin publicly praised Musk and spoke about Moscow’s contacts with him.
On Oct. 28, Putin called the SpaceX chief a “genius” and said Russia was in close contact with US partners, including Musk, to prevent satellites from interfering with one another.
Putin made the remarks while discussing Russia’s effort to build a satellite internet network to rival Starlink. He said Russia had launched more than 30 satellites and was only taking its first steps. Putin did not connect those comments to the communications Zelensky described from the start of the full-scale invasion.
The latest dispute began after restrictions imposed overnight on Oct. 13-14 disrupted Ukrainian drone operations, particularly interceptor drones used against Russian jet-powered Shaheds.
Musk said the US military, including President Donald Trump, set the speed limits on Starshield – Zelensky said Russia was trying to exploit the outage. The exchange was detailed as Ukraine reported that the US controlled Starshield limits .
On Oct. 20, the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk ordered the restrictions , citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.
On Oct. 21, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Starlink access was governed by a private commercial contract and that decisions rested with SpaceX and Musk, not the White House, as detailed in Rubio’s comments on access.
A Ukrainian defense ministry source said on Oct. 23 that the military was still recording losses at 161 kph (100 mph) and had no confirmation the restrictions had been lifted.
On Oct. 24, Musk acknowledged SpaceX had throttled Starlink and alleged Ukraine had violated the commercial service’s terms by using it for offensive drone strikes. Ukrainian defense figures disputed the allegation and said the civilian service’s speed limits and geofencing made such use technically implausible. Their response to Musk’s terms-of-service claim set out the dispute.
Ukraine later said Starlink and Starshield had returned to full operation. On Oct. 28, the Pentagon inspector general declined a bipartisan request to investigate the disruptions, saying the Air Force was better placed to address the concerns. The request came from nine senators who wanted to know whether US officials had directed or known in advance about changes affecting Ukraine’s satellite access.
Zelensky also said Ukraine retaliated after Russian hackers attacked the country’s Air Alert app, which had sent users false warnings about radiation and chemical threats. He confirmed Kyiv responded by targeting Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry app, following the attack on Ukraine’s Air Alert app .
Asked about Trump, Zelensky described their relationship as “emotional” and urged Washington to put greater pressure on Putin rather than Ukraine. He also spoke about how Russia’s invasion had taken childhood from Ukrainian children, including his 13-year-old son, Kyrylo, in his remarks on the war’s impact on children .
Zelensky said lifting Starshield restrictions could help Ukraine locate Russian ballistic missile launchers before they fire. He said he had raised the request with Trump three or four times and would use the system to target launch sites, not energy facilities, as he explained when discussing the missile-launcher targets .

articles.title_orig: CVS to break up $117 billion business, separating pharmacies from insurance; shares fall
articles.title_zh: CVS to break up $117 billion business, separating pharmacies from insurance; shares fall
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health said Wednesday it is splitting into two companies, marking one of the largest shakeups in the healthcare industry. It’s a major reversal of the mergers that brought together the nation’s largest drugstore retailer along with health insurance giant Aetna and pharmacy benefit manager Caremark.
One company, which would house CVS’s 9,000 retail pharmacies, mail order pharmacy, specialty drug business and MinuteClinic, will be named CVS Pharmacy.
The other, comprising of Aetna, Caremark and two companies that CVS acquired that provide primary care and in-home health evaluations to senior citizens, will be called CVS Health in the interim.
The separation is expected to close in early 2028.
The breakup unwinds a strategy that began in 2007, when CVS merged with Caremark, which handles prescription benefits available to people with health insurance. In 2018, CVS acquired Aetna for $69 billion.
“We’re basically taking what I believe is one great company and making it two,” said CVS CEO David Joyner in a statement Wednesday.
The company split will have little impact on the way people shop at CVS – the company didn’t announce any closures as part of the news – nor will affect what patients pay for prescriptions.
Pharmacy benefit management businesses work on the backend, negotiating directly with drugmakers on the cost of prescription drugs. But CVS’s drugstores and Caremark insurance operate separately. Splitting into two companies won’t change how they function.
The split does, however, mark a major step back from the widespread trend to integrate various parts of the healthcare industry – including insurers, pharmacy benefit managers and providers – into massive conglomerates. That consolidation has come under attack from consumer advocates and state and federal lawmakers for wielding too much control of the sector, leading to higher costs for patients. Some members of Congress have called for breaking up the companies.
Also, health insurers have come under cost pressure because Americans are using more healthcare services. Meanwhile, lawmakers and regulators are seeking to reform the pharmacy benefit manager industry just as it contends with new players looking to chip away at the dominance of Caremark and other major PBMs.
Meanwhile, CVS’ retail business has been hampered by consumers shifting to online channels, where the company still lags leaders like Amazon, Michael Cherny, an analyst with Leerink Partners, wrote in a client note on Tuesday evening after reports of the split surfaced.
Cherny, who called the news “a complete shock,” wrote that CVS’ pharmacy business has been performing well so “perhaps the outlook for a standalone retail pharmacy (still with meaningful scale and leverage on its own) is stronger now than before.”
Joyner, who will lead the new CVS Health company, took over as CEO in 2024 in the wake of layoffs, store closings and poor stock performance.
Shares of CVS Health, which have risen since Joyner’s appointment, fell 12% in midday trading after initially ticking up in premarket trading. Shareholders will get shares of both companies in a tax-free transaction, according to the company.
CVS also reported higher third-quarter earnings and revenue Wednesday, due primarily to better results from its Health Care Benefits segment. The company also raised its earnings guidance for the rest of this year.
CVS has 9,000 locations across the United States, 800 of which operate “MinuteClinics” staffed by nurse practitioners and physician assistants. It has 30,000 pharmacists and 200,000 employees in its stores, the company said during an earnings call Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Israel's president takes first steps on building new government after accepting election results
articles.title_zh: Israel's president takes first steps on building new government after accepting election results
articles.content_orig:
Move comes after attorney general blocks Shin Bet call to interrogate politicians from Palestinian-led parties
Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of last week’s vote that stripped Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition of its governing majority, rejecting claims of mass fraud promoted by the prime minister.
The main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, said Netanyahu had launched a “pogrom against democracy” in attempting to hold on to power by discrediting valid votes and weaponising security forces against parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel .
Hours earlier, Israel’s attorney general said she had blocked a demand from the Shin Bet security service to interrogate senior politicians from the Palestinian-led parties because she had not been presented with any evidence of wrongdoing.
“In a country governed by the rule of law, neither citizens nor elected officials can be interrogated without evidence that justifies doing so,” Gali Baharav-Miara said in a statement, after Haaretz reported on the attempt to target four politicians.
Election authorities on Wednesday presented the final results to the president, Isaac Herzog, after rejecting allegations they had been tainted by large-scale foreign interference and voter fraud.
“The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the Central Elections Committee said in a statement.
The body’s chair, Noam Sohlberg, said some “suspicions” were still under investigation but “they do not cast doubt on the election as a whole or justify delaying the election results”.
When the results were handed over, Herzog denounced racist attacks on Palestinian citizens who had turned out to vote at historic rates.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said. “I hold Arab society in Israel in great respect. I value its contribution to the country in every area of life, and its desire to integrate.”
Herzog will play a key role in the formation of the next government by choosing which politician has the first chance to create a coalition. He is expected to name Eisenkot, and the announcement could come as early as Thursday evening.
A former leader of the Israeli military who lost his son fighting in Gaza, Eisenkot has secured the public support of all of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties. Palestinian-led parties have said their priority is removing Netanyahu, so they are expected to back him as the strongest contender to achieve that.
However, negotiations could take weeks and Eisenkot warned of ongoing attempts to undermine trust in the election results. He accused Netanyahu of weaponising the security services against domestic opponents in an effort to hold on to power.
“The employees of the Ministry of Defense, law enforcement and the civil service in Israel are servants of the state, not the king,” he said in a statement. “Woe to anyone who abuses their authority and role for political considerations.”
The Shin Bet chief, David Zini, handpicked for the role by Netanyahu, had ordered the interrogations and sought to classify the investigation as a security file, which would have allowed harsher conditions including barring the politicians from having legal counsel.
Nadav Eyal, an Israeli journalist and commentator, said the public should brace for more extreme attempts to dismiss election results and discredit the leading opposition parties.
“The groundwork is steadily being laid for violence,” he wrote on X. “What you’re hearing breaking right now is the foundation of the legal and governmental orders in Israel.”
Netanyahu presided over a racist campaign targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel – about 20% of the population – and on election day began promoting the unfounded accusations of mass fraud now rejected by election authorities.
Ahmad Tibi, one of the most prominent and effective Palestinian politicians, was reportedly among those the Shin Bet sought to interrogate. He responded to the latest allegations, as news broke of sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterms, with a swipe at Netanyahu’s fear of democracy.
“[The] attorney general is checking suspicion of ties between the Joint List and Democrats in the US,” Tibi wrote in a social media post. “According to the suspicion, in both cases the same sophisticated method was employed: people arrived in droves at the polling stations, cast a slip, and went home.”

articles.title_orig: Google Tries to Walk Back Controversial School AI Policy Following Political Backlash
articles.title_zh: Google Tries to Walk Back Controversial School AI Policy Following Political Backlash
articles.content_orig:
Students using Google software in schools will not be allowed to use Google search unless their school system also provides them access to artificial intelligence tools
Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company's search engine unless their school system also opts in to artificial intelligence tools , the tech giant said Tuesday.
The Mountain View, California, company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom.
On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators and that opting out of AI tools would also mean losing access to Google search.
Access to Google's AI features — Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Gemini in Classroom — as well as Google search will be automatically turned off for K-12 student accounts until “school administrators explicitly turn them on,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post .
“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Phillips wrote.
Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.
Google faced an outcry in August when it switched on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.
Tuesday's announcement was met with swift criticism from educators and policymakers.
“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”
Messages seeking additional comment from Google were left on Tuesday.
New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation's biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.
Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick, easy answers to questions instead of thinking critically. And experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children’s brain development .
Josh Golin, executive director of children's advocacy group Fairplay, said Google's attempt to “strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.” He said Google's technology in schools is not about learning but about “developing lifetime brand loyalty” for its products.
“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available," Golin said in a statement.
Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and "use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”

Investors are being offered slices of SpaceX's $40 billion chip financing worth up to $500 million ahead of the formal sale process, as concerns over AI spending and potential political scrutiny cloud the sector's outlook, Bloomberg noted.
The package, announced in October, secured investor commitments before pricing was finalized, leaving lenders exposed to market swings as they seek buyers. It reportedly includes an $8.3 billion senior-secured loan for banks and several bond tranches for asset managers. Together with a $7 billion lease prepayment, the financing would cover about $47.3 billion of Nvidia equipment, including its next-generation Rubin chips.
SpaceX signed a binding commitment in October for an Apollo-managed entity to buy computing equipment and lease it to the company. The agreement is expected to be finalized before year-end, with deliveries and leases beginning in the first half of 2027.
Each equipment batch would carry a lease lasting roughly five to five-and-a-quarter years. SpaceX expects to pay about $40 billion in principal, plus interest and other expenses. Called as the largest committed GPU financing, the deal would expand computing capacity for Grok and cloud customers. Several major investment firms have also committed funding.
The chips would reportedly be owned by a separate financing vehicle that issues the debt, helping protect SpaceX's corporate credit ratings. SpaceX would still have to pay rent if the equipment is damaged or unforeseen events disrupt operations.
"Rent is owed regardless of equipment condition, casualty or force majeure, providing investors with a clean look-through to SpaceX credit," an investor presentation reportedly stated.
The financing push comes as Republicans warn that Democratic control of Congress could bring greater scrutiny of Musk and other business leaders who worked with President Donald Trump.
U.S. Sen.Ted Cruz, a Republican from Texas, warned during the All-In podcast's election-night coverage that Musk could face congressional subpoenas. "I will say also, look, the Democrats have already foreshadowed that if they have one or both houses, they're going to use subpoenas to go after business executives who've worked with the president, to go after Elon Musk," Cruz said.
"They've already declared they intend to engage in lawfare and in open attacks," he added. Cruz also warned of growing opposition to AI and data centers, saying that slowing construction could damage the economy.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, separately warned that Texas' incoming Democratic attorney general could target Musk, raising concerns over Tesla's Gigafactory near Austin. "They're going to go after Elon Musk. I guarantee you they will do that," DeSantis said at a Wednesday press conference. He warned that political hostility could complicate Musk's business operations in Texas.
Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson, a Democratic state senator, defeated Republican state Sen.Mayes Middleton to become the first Democrat elected to the office since 1994.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave Bonds Hit Lows as Texas Data Centers in Crosshairs
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Bonds Hit Lows as Texas Data Centers in Crosshairs
articles.content_orig:
Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total in Tuesday’s elections
Track live results from all 50 states
Send us your questions about the US midterms results and Democrats’ ‘blue wave’
There were three big losers in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US: Donald Trump, Elon Musk and datacenters.
Datacenters, the facilities full of semiconductor chips that power artificial intelligence and a host of other online products, were on the ballot in elections in at least 40 jurisdictions across 10 states. Voters responded with a strong rebuke of the giant buildings, which have has become a symbol of the tech industry and AI.
In Ohio alone, at least 14 municipalities passed bans or restrictions on datacenter development, including in Sunbury, where Amazon has proposed a $2m datacenter project. In Maine, eight municipalities passed temporary datacenter moratoriums. In Emporio, Kansas, where a 1,000-acre gigawatt-scale datacenter was recently proposed, a ban on high-impact datacenters was approved by voters.
Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total, with one notable exception: Hardwood, North Dakota. The small city of a population of less than 1,000 people voted down a bill that would impose restrictions on datacenter development.
Where datacenters were not explicitly on the ballot, officials who have pushed back against their development were elected. In Texas , Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who secured a historical victory as governor on Tuesday night over her Republican opponent, has promised to impose moratoriums on their construction. She has pledged to implement greater restrictions on and community input into whether datacenters can be built. Towards the end of his tenure, Greg Abbott, her Republican opponent, had also tried to capitalize on anti-datacenter sentiment, demanding an end to electricity subsidies for them. He reversed his previous stance that had welcomed datacenters to the state.
Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became governor of Georgia, and Amy Acton, the newly elected governor of Ohio , have also pledged to implement moratoria on the construction of large datacenters.
Anti-datacenter sentiment has grown in the last few months has become a bipartisan issue. In May, Florida governor Ron DeSantis signed a bill imposing strict regulations on large-scale datacenters. Still, last night’s election solidified the overwhelming opposition to these centers of compute that have come to serve as a stand-in for the ultra wealthy and resource extraction by the AI industry.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Elon Musk, who poured over $400m into supporting conservative candidates, posted on X.
Analyst Dan Ives said the results of the midterms are a clear sign that the pace of datacenter buildout will start to slow down.
after newsletter promotion
“There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next two years,” Ives said. Ives said he was particularly worried about Hinojosa who is a “known anti-datacenter politician”.
“The biggest worry of the night for tech investors and the AI trade was around the state of Texas where 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from,” he said.

articles.title_orig: E.l.f. Beauty posts 51% sales increase, raises full-year guidance
articles.title_zh: E.l.f. Beauty posts 51% sales increase, raises full-year guidance
articles.content_orig:
E.l.f. Beauty on Wednesday blew past Wall Street expectations as it posted a 51% increase in net sales in its second fiscal quarter.
The beauty company said it saw its 31st consecutive quarter of net sales growth, attributing the streak to strong performance across its portfolio. The revenue spike was driven by both retail and e-commerce channels across the U.S. and internationally, the company added.
"The thing I'm most pleased about is we saw strength across our entire portfolio," CEO Tarang Amin told CNBC in an interview. "Every one of our brands contributed strong growth this quarter."
Amin added that E.l.f. is the most-searched brand on TikTok Shop and the No. 2 brand in cosmetics on the platform. The company also said it saw strong results for Rhode, the skincare brand it acquired last year.
The company raised its full fiscal-year guidance following the better-than-anticipated quarter. It now expects net sales in the range of $2 billion to $2.03 billion, compared with a previous range of between $1.94 billion and $1.97 billion. It also upped its adjusted EBITDA projection to a range of $421 million to $427 million from between $401 million and $407 million.
E.l.f. said it now expects adjusted earnings per share for the year to come in between $3.82 and $3.86, exceeding prior guidance of between $3.50 and $3.55 per share. It's also expecting a net income range of $231 million to $233 million, up from a previous range of $212 million to $215 million.
It had already raised its guidance last quarter after outperforming its expectations.
Amin said the company is "very bullish" on the holiday season, expecting high sales through the end of the year.
Here's how the company performed in its second fiscal quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the period ended Sept. 30, E.l.f. reported net income of $30.03 million, or 50 cents per share, up significantly from roughly $3 million, or 5 cents per share, the year prior.
Net sales grew 51% to $520.8 million.
E.l.f. also saw significant growth in its international channels, with business up 165%. Amin told CNBC that only 25% of the company's business is outside of the U.S. and that it has a "tremendous opportunity" to build on that momentum.
The company also said its gross margin increased 1.6% during the quarter, including a 0.3% benefit from tariff refunds. Amin previously said the retailer planned to fully reinvest that money into pricing and marketing to continue driving growth.
Though E.l.f. received most of its refunds in its first fiscal quarter, some of those funds flowed through the second quarter, and the company expects to receive a yearly total of around $55 million. Amin told CNBC on Wednesday that the company lowered the price of about 10% of its units by $1 because of the tariff benefits.
"We're seeing great unit momentum based on that," he said.
