articles.title_orig: WoW: Forever May Have Just Sneakily Revealed New Class And Race Combos
articles.title_zh: WoW: Forever May Have Just Sneakily Revealed New Class And Race Combos
articles.content_orig:
Whether you’re stepping into World of Warcraft for the first time or finding your way back to Azeroth, there’s a place for you in World of Warcraft: Forever . Explore a new and reimagined Azeroth at your own pace, discover new places or revisit old favorites, and meet fellow adventurers along the way. This permanent home alongside modern and Classic WoW puts community first and makes the journey as meaningful as the destination.
Set after the events of Warcraft III Reforged: Forsaken Kingdom and before Molten Core, WoW: Forever takes you across the original continents on an adventure to level 60. Your journey continues through new stories, experiences, and updates inspired by years of player passion and feedback.
WoW: Forever expands the Eastern Kingdoms and Kalimdor with new and reimagined zones and more than 1,000 new quests across the level 1–60 journey. Explore new destinations including Mount Hyjal, Shen’dralas, the Riverglades, and Zephras Isle.
Mount Hyjal invites you to explore the aftermath of Archimonde’s defeat, journey through Darkwhisper Gorge, and help shape the future of a recovering land. In Shen'dralas, a long-hidden mystery between Mulgore and Desolace becomes a new adventure tied to the Shen’dralar, Eldre’Thalas, Dire Maul, and the centaur tribes of the region.
In the Riverglades, you’ll discover a rugged frontier of rivers, grasslands, trade routes, struggling communities, and old grudges, with more than 150 new quests across much of the mid-30s to mid-40s experience. On Zephras Isle, you’ll begin an elemental skybound starting experience from levels 1 through 12, blending Classic Warcraft aesthetics with architecture inspired by Skywall.
Race and class shape the hero you become in World of Warcraft: Forever , from the fantasy you embody to the role you take on in the world. You can return to a familiar favorite, explore a newly available combination, or begin your journey as a Skyborne character, with each choice offering a different way to step into Azeroth’s next chapter.
The Skyborne are a new playable race in World of Warcraft: Forever , bringing their own identity to the unfolding story. When choosing to play this new race, players can choose between Horde-aligned Windshapers which can become Shaman, or an Alliance-aligned High-Order Skyborne which can become Mages.
World of Warcraft: Forever opens new ways to build your character, including Orc Mages, Troll Warlocks, Undead Paladins, Human Hunters, Gnome Priests, Dwarf Shamans, and the debut of the Skyborne. Explore the possibilities and learn more in our article .
The Skyborne—also known as the shen’dorei, or hidden people—are a new playable race in World of Warcraft: Forever. Their journey begins on Zephras Isle, a level 1–12 starting experience that blends classic Warcraft aesthetics with elemental architecture and a story shaped by wind and ancestry. At character creation, you’ll choose whether your Skyborne joins the proud Horde or the noble Alliance.
Get to know the Skyborne in our previously published article .
The first time you log in to World of Warcraft: Forever, you’ll be asked to Choose Your Experience Preset. You’ll make this choice before selecting your Ruleset.
A more traditional presentation with simpler visuals, standard character models, and fewer modern interface features enabled by default for a cleaner, more original-style experience with less automatic guidance.
An updated presentation with higher visual fidelity and additional interface features enabled by default.
If you are not sure which to choose, start with Enhanced. The preset gives you a convenient starting point rather than locking in your choices, and you can change its individual settings later under Game Menu > Options. After your initial log in to the game, you will no longer see this screen.
Each time you create a new character, you can select either High Definition (HD) or Standard Definition (SD) character models and animations. HD uses higher-detail models and updated visuals, while SD offers the style associated with the original look of World of Warcraft. This character-specific choice affects only appearance—not abilities or progression—and you can change it later in the Options Menu or by visiting a Barbershop in game.
Every journey through Azeroth begins with a choice about the kind of world you want to step into. In World of Warcraft: Forever , your journey starts with a Ruleset rather than a traditional realm-selection screen.
Instead of picking the “right” realm before creating a character, you choose the kind of experience you want in World of Warcraft: Forever . Each Ruleset functions as a broad player ecosystem rather than a single traditional realm, making it easier to find others who share your preferred playstyle while preserving the feeling of a living, active Azeroth.
For players seeking the ultimate challenge, where every decision matters and death carries lasting consequences, the Hardcore ruleset will become available sometime after launch.
Learn more about rulesets in our previously published article .
A name is one of the first choices you make when creating a character. It can be humorous, heroic, mysterious, deeply personal, or something that only makes sense to the friends who have adventured with you for years. In World of Warcraft: Forever , character names gain more room to breathe through a new two-name structure designed for a larger, realmless Azeroth.
Instead of relying on a single name tied to a specific realm, each character will have two names. Together, those parts form a full name that is unique within a region, creating more possibilities for players who want something that fits their character, history, or story in Azeroth. Learn more in our previously published article .
The Camping system in World of Warcraft: Forever turns the Cooking profession’s Basic Campfire into a shared campsite where adventurers can rest, prepare, and connect. Nearby players can contribute up to three profession-crafted Camp Features, with each player adding one. Sit or craft at a campsite for at least 1 minute to gain benefits from its Camp Features, including buffs that are mutually exclusive with their corresponding class buffs. Take a moment to meet fellow adventurers before returning to the road. Learn more in our previously published overview article .
World of Warcraft: Forever introduces an exciting new account-wide horizontal progression system—the Legacy System. It’s a whole new way to progress, focusing on exploring everything the game has to offer, rather than power progression alone.
This new system encourages players to level multiple characters of different classes and tradeskills and experience the journey all over again, however leveling alternate (alts) characters is not required to benefit from the system. All character advantages can be unlocked on a single character. The Legacy System has three major components: Legacy Challenges, Legacy Perks, and Legacy Rewards. Learn more in our overview article.
A spell to cast, an ally to heal, a well-earned reward to collect—there’s plenty to keep you busy in Azeroth. If you prefer a gamepad, World of Warcraft: Forever gives you another way to join the action.
In World of Warcraft: Forever , we’ve refined targeting, casting, looting, and menu navigation for gamepads while keeping the familiar feel players have come to know. Learn more in our overview article.
World of Warcraft: Forever introduces nine new five-player dungeons for adventurers from level 13 through level 60. Rooted in the original World of Warcraft , each dungeon brings new threats, quests, and adventures to the Eastern Kingdoms and Kalimdor. Learn more about each of the new additions in our previously published article .

articles.title_orig: French blood banks targeted by refrigerator cyberattack
articles.title_zh: French blood banks targeted by refrigerator cyberattack
articles.content_orig:
Blood banks in France were included among cyberattacks that hit refrigeration systems in several European countries on Sunday and Monday, French authorities said on Wednesday.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said that a " cybersecurity incident" targeted a refrigeration service provider affecting control systems at three cold storage sites for plasma and blood samples.
The cyberattack attempted to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but it was warded off before any damage could be done. The plasma in the affected refrigerators was transferred or secured, the EFS said.
"No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost," the EFS said in a statement, adding that its distribution operations were not interrupted.
The cyberattack was first reported on Wednesday by the French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaine , which said the temperatures had been programmed to reach a boiling 110 C (230 F), rather than -30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit).
"Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised," the EFS said.
France's cybersecurity agency and Health Ministry said an investigation is underway, but did not indicate who could have been responsible.
The Health Ministry said Wednesday that remote access to the affected refrigerators was disabled, and credited monitoring and alarm systems with ensuring the safety of blood supplies.
Coolworld, the company supplying the refrigeration equipment, said the vulnerability was related to a component from a "third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control."
On Sunday and Monday, a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at supermarkets in several European countries, including France and Germany, destroying large quantities of frozen food.
It was reminiscent of a similar attack three weeks ago targeting refrigeration systems at dozens of French supermarkets.
The attacks have cost supermarkets millions of euros in wasted food.
On Wednesday, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize said it expects the cyberattack in October to reduce quarterly sales by as much as €250 million ($281 million).
"While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations," CEO Franz Muller said.

The iPhone Duo has been shipping for a little while now, but plenty of iOS apps still haven't been adapted to its two displays. Google Maps is no longer one of them, as version 26.44.4 of the app is now being reported to add full support for the device.
While Google's App Store release notes only mention "bug fixes", if you already use Google Maps on the iPhone Duo, you'll notice the difference right away. Previously, the app was slightly offset to the left on the outer screen to make room for the new iOS dock position. On the inner screen, you got the regular iPhone app, which could be moved to the left or right but left most of the display empty.
Now, Google Maps fills both screens. That doesn't change much on the outer one, though it does look neater. On the inside, the app now has a wide layout, with the menus and search box on the left and the map or satellite view stretching corner to corner. That makes it a lot like Google Maps on the iPad.
Street View also benefits from the extra width. By default, it takes up the left side of the inner screen and leaves the right side for the map. There seemingly isn't a way to swap the two, but you can make Street View fill the whole screen. If you close the iPhone Duo while in Street View, it moves to the outer screen, and a close button takes you back to the map.

articles.title_orig: A nationwide backlash against data centers erupts at the polls
articles.title_zh: A nationwide backlash against data centers erupts at the polls
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state's first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies.
Texas is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers and was just one place where deep voter unease over the build-out was on display. Voters across the country passed a series of local ballot measures aimed at restricting construction in the years ahead.
Hinojosa, Texas's first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030.
"I want to say something to the powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state," she told supporters in her victory speech . "The voters have delivered a mandate for change, and it is change they will get."
Her victory was one of a series of wins for Democrats in Texas. The party is also on track to take control of the Texas House , which would give Hinojosa more power to follow through on restrictions even as the state Senate appears set to remain under Republican control.
"We view the Texas gubernatorial race as particularly important for the next leg of the AI trade," wrote Raymond James's Ed Mills in a pre-election note saying that a strong Democratic showing there "could signal a broader electoral wave while increasing concerns about data center moratoriums and more restrictive AI regulation in the nation's largest planned data center development."
Bank of America called the race "one of the highest impact elections for the entire utility sector."
Hinojosa made opposition to data center construction a central part of her campaign, charging in one ad that Gov. Greg Abbott "works for" Elon Musk.
She staked out plans for a moratorium on new data center construction, stricter regulations on water and power usage, and an end to tax breaks.
Abbott was seeking his fourth term as governor and said last year he wanted Texas to be the "epicenter of AI development."
More recently, he announced a moratorium of his own and said he would support more stringent requirements on power and water usage. Hinojosa immediately charged that Abbott's new proposals amounted to an "election year pause."
Tobin Marcus of Wolfe Research said Texas "is the one state with enough scale and enough difference between the candidates that it could make a real difference."
The race reflected a national mood that has turned sharply against data centers in recent months.
NBC exit polls on Tuesday showed that 57% of voters felt "AI will do more to hurt society" compared to just 24% who said it would help.
A UMass Amherst Poll in September also found nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose AI data center construction in their communities, with just 11% of voters welcoming them
On Tuesday, voters weighed in on data center ballot measures in contests spanning 13 states, from Arkansas to Wisconsin.
One tracker counted 28 measures before voters to limit data centers. On Wednesday morning, with votes still being counted, virtually every one was on track to pass. In Ohio alone, voters in at least 14 municipalities passed bans or other restrictions .
In the Ohio Senate race, voters elected Democrat Sherrod Brown, who, like Hinojosa, made opposition to data center construction a key part of his campaign message.
"I do not work for the utility companies, I do not work for data centers," Brown said as he declared victory on Tuesday night .
Even Elon Musk seemed to acknowledge the dour public sentiment toward data centers. He quipped in a post early Wednesday as the results became clear, "data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now."
This story has been updated.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Treasury Yields Fall on Election Results, Cheaper Oil
articles.title_zh: Treasury Yields Fall on Election Results, Cheaper Oil
articles.content_orig:
The electoral sweep by Democrats on Tuesday night injects a new, unstable dynamic into the single biggest political risk to financial markets in the coming year: the debt limit . Unless a defeated Republican Party makes a swift and unlikely show of unity to take the issue off the table in its last few weeks in power, the protracted fight that will unfold is set to be nastier than ever, adding volatility to an already shaky bond market.
Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results
Past episodes of brinkmanship around the need to raise the government's borrowing limit have involved Republicans in Congress demanding budget cuts from a Democratic president as the price of their vote. This time it will almost certainly be the left seeking concessions from the right.
The debt limit is the definition of a must-pass bill, even more than issues like funding the government and the defense budget. That makes it potentially the one real chance the new Democratic majority in Congress has to extract concessions from a president who is already pledging to veto their agenda. Markets will hate the entire process, even if — as many expect — it ends in compromise.
Because it is Democrats who hold the leverage, unlike past episodes, the ultimate agreement is more likely to increase government spending than lower it. With high bond yields weighing on the economy, and Americans expecting action from a newly empowered Democratic opposition, the fight could be particularly damaging.
Many in the markets are stuck on the outdated idea that Democrats are less assertive than Republicans, said Aniket Shah, head of the Washington policy team at the investment bank Jefferies.
"They have this sort of mental image of Biden-Harris 2024," said Shah. "I don't think they realize how aggressively Democrats plan to take 2027."
The debt ceiling is a quirk of the congressional budgeting process. It stops the government from borrowing funds that Congress has already ordered federal agencies to spend. And because Congress has run deficits for decades — this year at $1.99 trillion — the pile of debt periodically bumps into the debt ceiling.
Congress last set the limit in 2025, when it gave the Treasury Department the authority to borrow $41.1 trillion. The Treasury is likely to hit its maximum borrowing capacity by midsummer, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center , a nonprofit that tracks the issue.
The Treasury can use budgeting techniques to extend the so-called X-date, when the U.S. would no longer be able to meet all its obligations, to sometime in the fourth quarter of 2027, according to Wall Street estimates.
A few technical hiccups aside, the U.S. has never meaningfully breached the debt limit. The results of the U.S. missing payments would be chaotic as damage ripples out across the financial system into the global economy. U.S. default would immediately call into question trillions in Treasury securities that are the lifeblood of the global financial system. Damaging them could send the U.S. and global economies into an economic tailspin with no obvious means of recovery.
Because the stakes are so high, Shah and many others on Wall Street have come to believe that the episode will produce volatility but will ultimately be resolved in compromise.
Fights under former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden saw Republican congressional majorities use the issue to ram through spending reductions. (The 2025 raise was less contentious, because Republicans held Congress and the presidency. It was passed along party lines.)
Still, the risk-taking in those episodes contributed to ratings firms' decisions to downgrade U.S. debt — and could again.
President Donald Trump has called for Republicans to resolve the issue in the next few weeks, before the new Democratic-majority Congress is seated.
That isn't likely. The 2025 debt limit increase only passed because it was tied to a package of tax cuts and other policy changes. Republican debt hawks complained but held their noses.
Republicans may attempt to raise the limit in the coming lame-duck session under a budgeting procedure called reconciliation, which would allow them to move ahead without Democrats' votes. But success would require unity among a fractured, fleeting Republican majority that also faces several other more pressing priorities.
The most likely path toward raising the debt limit is the incoming Democratic majority negotiating another temporary fix with Trump. But they aren't going to make it easy. The president has occasionally made noises about making deals, but the political incentives ahead of the 2028 presidential election are for both sides to dig in.
"[Democrats] are going to want to embarrass the White House, and they're going to want to get leverage," Shah said. Democrats will use that to push to reverse cuts to Medicaid spending passed in 2025 and to try to restore healthcare spending, he said.
Democrats could also seek to tie the debt limit to restraining signature Trump policies, such as limiting the war with Iran or rolling back tariffs, analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a research note Wednesday.
Another potential compromise being considered in some corners of Washington is for Democrats to tie an increase in the corporate tax rate to a debt limit raise, said George Pollack, senior U.S. analyst with Signum Global Advisors. Trump has shown he can be surprisingly flexible on similar issues, Pollack noted.
That is what will make this debt limit fight different. In the past, Republicans used it to try to win spending reductions they couldn't get through regular budget negotiations. Now Democrats will broaden it out into an all-purpose hostage. That effort is far more likely to raise overall government spending than cut it. "There's a very weird irony here," said Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at PGIM, an asset manager.
The path to compromise will likely be rocky. Sockin believes it may turn out like the 2025 government shutdown. That was the longest government-wide shutdown in history, even though Democrats weren't in control of either chamber of Congress. This time they will have even more power.
If the fight extends beyond the X-date, missing debt payments could do serious damage to the financial system.
"It's not our base case, but we think the risk is higher than ever that you could get a technical default from the government," Sockin said. That would see the U.S. miss a payment, even if the government eventually makes it up.
That would still hurt. "You'll get more downgrades to the U.S. sovereign, and those might bite more this time," Sockin said. Yields on longer-term Treasurys would rise to account for added uncertainty.
Crossing the red line could prompt a "very negative reaction in equity markets," he said.
The coming months will show just how close Democrats are willing to get to that line.

articles.title_orig: Serbia detains police officers over alleged use of force against protesters
articles.title_zh: Serbia detains police officers over alleged use of force against protesters
articles.content_orig:
Nine people, among them the commander of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit (SAJ) Igor Zmiric , were detained on Wednesday evening for up to 48 hours on suspicion of abusing and torturing students in the Serbian Government garage in August 2025. The detention order was issued by officers of the Internal Control Sector of the Interior Ministry (MUP), on the instruction of a public prosecutor from the First Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade. It is the first arrest in the “Garage” case.
In its statement, the ministry gives initials and birth years rather than names. According to it, those detained are I. Z. (1979), B. J. (1978), D. V. (1978), J. O. (1983), V. L. (1978), N. D. (1976), N. F. (1973) and Z. V. (1972), all police officers, along with a civilian, M. V. (1978), who was a police officer at the time of the events. Media report that the first set of initials belongs to Zmiric, and Srpskainfo names him in full. All of them are suspects, not convicts: a decision to detain someone is not a verdict.
They are suspected of abuse and torture, committed jointly, as members of the Unit for the Protection of Certain Persons and Facilities (JZO). The MUP describes the event this way:
The offense was committed in such a way that the suspects, on August 14-15, 2025, from about 10:30 p.m. to 1:00 a.m. in Belgrade, in the garage of the Government of the Republic of Serbia building in Nemanjina Street, used force and threats to inflict great pain and severe suffering on a number of injured persons, with the aim of obtaining information from them, intimidating them and punishing them unlawfully
The ministry has released neither the number nor the names of the injured parties. All those detained will be brought before the on-duty prosecutor for questioning within the legal deadline.
The daily Danas, citing several sources in the MUP, reports that Zmiric’s deputy was also taken in. Asked by the newsroom, the MUP replied that only the prosecutor’s office handling the case could have such information, so the ministry has not confirmed that detail. The descriptions differ, the total does not: the MUP speaks of eight police officers and one former officer, KRIK of Zmiric, seven serving officers and one former officer, and Danas of Zmiric, his deputy and seven others. Every account adds up to nine people.
The case is tied to Nikolina Sindjelic, a student at the Faculty of Political Sciences. Right after the events, on August 15, 2025, she told N1 that she and her colleague Stevan Zdravkovic were seized by JZO members, police and masked men as they were returning from a protest along Nemanjina Street. They were taken into the Government garage, where, she said, they had to lie on the floor and look down. They spent about three hours in the garage, then about two hours at a police station in Majke Jevrosime Street.
Sindjelic said at the time that JZO commander Marko Kricak slapped her, struck her head against a wall and threatened her:
He kept saying he would strip me and rape me in front of everyone
According to KRIK, Kricak was arrested a few days ago, but in a separate case, Senjak, on suspicion of abusing his position in a murder investigation. Sindjelic named Zmiric in her criminal complaint. She had earlier described him to Nova.rs with the words: “He behaved extremely cruelly.” The same outlet reported in November 2025 that Zmiric, until then deputy commander of the JZO, had been appointed SAJ commander.
Al Jazeera Balkans reports that in late August 2025 the police answered a prosecutor’s request by saying that surveillance camera footage from the garage does not exist because it is deleted automatically. The same outlet writes that the Supreme Public Prosecutor issued a mandatory instruction for urgent action in the case on Monday, November 2.
After news of the arrest broke, Sindjelic told the FoNet agency that she expects a wider proceeding:
I hope that everyone who took part in it will be held responsible, precisely because my colleague Dusan was also in that torture.
She added that she hopes the people who mistreated the other students will be identified:
I hope work will also be done on identifying the people who mistreated them too.
Zmiric’s name was already linked in public to a KRIK investigation from February 2026, which reported that he was becoming the owner of a villa in the Avalske Doline neighborhood worth more than 400,000 euros. The investor, Nenad Sekularac, then confirmed to KRIK that he is building the villa for him and is “helping” him.
According to the MUP, the suspects will be brought before the competent prosecutor’s office within the legal deadline.
Još nema komentara. Budi prvi i podeli mišljenje.

articles.title_orig: Gold Prices Are Above $4,000 After Democrats Win Big in Midterm Elections
articles.title_zh: Gold Prices Are Above $4,000 After Democrats Win Big in Midterm Elections
articles.content_orig:
America's billionaires woke up Wednesday to a political reckoning — and a Wall Street rally.
As Democrats celebrated a sweeping midterm victory , some of the country's wealthiest donors traded barbs over record election spending . Others warned the results could threaten the artificial intelligence boom.
Wall Street, however, cheered the outcome. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4%, as investors welcomed political gridlock , reduced uncertainty and President Donald Trump's willingness to accept the results.
Virgin Group founder Richard Branson took aim at the billions spent influencing the election.
"I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent," Branson wrote Wednesday on LinkedIn , calling for campaign finance reform. Branson did not give donations that met the threshold reporting in the 2026 election cycle.
His comments came as Elon Musk, the election's largest individual donor , watched his preferred Republicans lose the Texas Senate and governor races despite pouring $224 million into the state — nearly half his record $474 million in political giving nationwide, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records.
Early Wednesday, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO suggested on X that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing before joking that his "election-interfering space lasers" had failed.
LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman , another major political donor, took a sharper tone.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote late Tuesday on X , accusing Musk of spending "outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power" while defending his own contributions to Democrats.
Other Democratic megadonors celebrated. "The world changed yesterday," Alex Soros wrote Wednesday on X, hailing the results as a generational victory after his family contributed roughly $103 million to Democratic political efforts.
But beyond the political sparring, some of the country's richest investors were focused on a potentially bigger consequence of the Democratic sweep : the future of the AI boom .
Even before polls closed Tuesday, Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman warned on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that slowing AI development could jeopardize America's technological edge. "Practically speaking, we can't slow down," he said.
As results rolled in Tuesday night, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya sounded an even starker warning.
Palihapitiya initially questioned whether the early results would hold, but warned that if they did, the implications for the AI trade could be severe.
"And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers," Palihapitiya said during an election-night livestream of the "All-In" podcast.
Texas offered an early test of those fears. Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has proposed a moratorium on new data-center construction until stronger safeguards are established, defeated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.
During the same livestream, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner warned the Democratic wave could mean at least 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI data-center capacity would not come online in 2027. Wall Street analyst Dan Ives estimated Wednesday that 10% of planned U.S. data centers would no longer go ahead.
AMD CEO Lisa Su acknowledged the growing resistance to AI's expansion , urging technology companies to demonstrate the benefits of data centers to local communities.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," Su told CNBC Wednesday .
Yet Wall Street may have found opportunity in the same slowdown that worried AI's biggest backers.
Fewer new data centers could increase the value of existing facilities while easing the enormous spending burden on technology giants. Big Tech stocks surged Wednesday , adding more than $750 billion in market value at one point, even as smaller, debt-dependent data-center operators tumbled.

articles.title_orig: Death toll hits 40 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, dozens remain missing
articles.title_zh: Death toll hits 40 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, dozens remain missing
articles.content_orig:
The death toll from a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday has risen to 40, ⁠with dozens still missing, officials said, in one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year.
The attack came a day after a brief U.S.-brokered local ceasefire expired and less than a week before the United States is due to bring together Ukrainian and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi for talks on ending the war , now in its fifth year.
Reuters footage on Wednesday showed men in military fatigues loading bodies in white plastic bags into the back of a ⁠van in the village of Komyshuvakha, which was struck multiple times.
Excavators were ​digging ⁠up earth near a huge blast crater while rescue workers searched underground for bodies.
Ivan Fedorov, the co-head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Defense Council, wrote on Telegram that 59 people were missing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Russian forces first dropped aerial ⁠bombs on an underground school building being used as a distribution point as people arrived to collect aid, then struck the ​shelter with ⁠more bombs.
Classes have long since been suspended at the ‌school because of its proximity to the front — Komyshuvakha lies some 11 miles from the nearest Russian positions — but it served as a shelter and handed out humanitarian aid every Monday, Zelenskyy said.
Two members of a rescue crew and four police officers were among the ‌dead, emergency services said.
Russia’s defense ministry said the attack targeted Ukrainian military units around ‌Komyshuvakha and two other settlements, and that up to 25 Ukrainian servicemen were killed.
Russia and Ukraine both deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Bodycam footage from one of the policemen killed in the attack, which Ukrainian police posted and Reuters verified, shows rubble and badly damaged buildings in the aftermath of the initial aerial attacks.
The policeman said the area was ⁠under threat from drones and appears to take shelter briefly inside the shell of a bombed-out building.
Later in the footage, 15 to 20 people in civilian clothing are gathered outside the entrance to an underground shelter when a warning comes over a radio that Russian glide bombs are heading in the direction of the village.
Residents rush down several flights of stairs and towards a room, while the policeman with the bodycam turns through a door into what appears to be a temporary police station.
Three other men and a woman are visible in the final frames before there is a large explosion and the camera turns black.
In a social media post accompanying the footage, the national police ‌said several strikes hit the area, including from a 3-ton FAB bomb, which is a large bomb fitted with ​a glide kit that allows it to fly long distances after being dropped from a Russian warplane.
According to defense intelligence ‌websites, a 3-ton glide bomb would carry around 1.4 tons of ⁠explosives.
The strike occurred a day after a six-day ceasefire to evacuate civilians from the ⁠Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky expired.
The truce, brokered by first lady Melania Trump , allowed nearly 800 people to be evacuated, according to the first lady. Zelenskyy awarded Trump a state honour for her ​role.
The United States will bring together delegations from Ukraine and Russia in ‌Abu Dhabi on November 10 to 11 to discuss ending ​the conflict, postwar security agreements and de-escalation, US envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.

articles.title_orig: ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results
articles.title_zh: ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
Democrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Projected results have provided the party with a number of things to celebrate - and rival Republicans some reasons to commiserate .
Here is everything you need to know about some of the big Democratic wins and some historic firsts .
Democrats have tallied up victories in states that were comfortably won by Trump two years ago in the presidential election.
With James Talarico winning a seat in the US Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa being elected state governor, Democrats scored two statewide victories in Texas - ending a string of defeats they have endured for almost two generations.
James Talarico, the new US senator in Texas, and Gina Hinojosa, the state's new governor, toast their successes
Talarico's supporters went beserk as the projected results arrived at an election-night party, wrote the BBC's Gary O'Donoghue. Attendees hugged, kissed and drank to a reality they dared not believe would come true.
Hinojosa became the first Latina to be elected governor of the state.
Among the other states where history was made by the Democrats were Kansas, where Adam Hamilton took a closely-fought Senate seat - giving the state its first Democratic senator for nearly a century.

Senior party figures who cheered the results included Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the Speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.
"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.
If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next Speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Johnson and becoming the first black person to fill that role.
Trump spoke throughout the evening to a number of US media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone and conceding that the Democrats did a "good job" .
He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Congress.
Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."
He acknowledged that the US-Israel war on Iran, which has impacted consumer prices in the US, had affected the vote. Trump argued that high fuel prices meant voters could not see how well his economy was doing "as much as they should have", adding: "The gasoline was caused by Iran."
Listen to Americast: Democrats make historic shift in US politics
Abdul El-Sayed has become the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate - after claiming victory in Michigan in what was one of a handful of closely fought contests. His win means the seat stays in Democratic hands.
He defeated Republican opponent Mike Rogers , who received the surprise backing of El-Sayed's Democratic rival in the primary contest, Haley Stevens, who changed her endorsement at the eleventh hour.
The race was one of the bitterest of the midterms. Trump invoked 9/11 and even called El-Sayed a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.
El-Sayed triumphed in one of the bitterest contests of the midterms
El-Sayed's supporters went wild when he took the stage to celebrate his claimed victory, wrote the BBC's Nada Tawfik. He said: "Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say 'inshallah,' or 'God willing,' whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned."
He went on to say: "But today, tonight, we can turn that 'inshallah' into 'alhamdulillah'. For the right-wing ops, that just means 'praise be to God.'"
The defeat of Susan Collins, who has served as the Republican senator for Maine for three decades, was one indicator of the scale of the Republican losses.
She was felled by Democratic candidate Troy Jackson , a logger who sought to point to his background to persuade blue-collar Mainers to vote for him.
In a statement reported by US media, Collins conceded defeat and said it had been the "honour of my life" to serve the state for 30 years.
The BBC's Helena Humphrey described a sombre atmosphere at Collins's watch party in the city of Maine - where the song Closing Time was played.
There was a sombre atmosphere at the watch party for Republican Susan Collins
Collins entered the race as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election, and found that her tactic to distance herself from Trump did not work.
Ashley Hinson suffered the same fate in Iowa, losing that closely-fought Senate seat to Josh Turek. Hinson had slightly distanced herself from the president, urging him to end the war with Iran and breaking with him on easing beef tariffs, while at the same time defending Trump's broader tariff policies as important.
Among the other firsts of the night were in Florida, where Republican Byron Donalds has become the state's first black governor , following a hearty endorsement from Trump.
Donalds, who will take over the job from Ron DeSantis, said his state was the "envy of the nation", and that he would work to make the state more affordable.
The result was one of the few high points of an otherwise difficult evening for the Republicans.
A win for Bryon Donalds in Florida was one of the few high points for Republicans
In the neighbouring state of Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, won the governor's race, becoming the first black governor and first woman to be elected to the state's highest office.
The BBC's Carl Nasman described ecstatic scenes as the race was projected blue. Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman and healthcare executive. The state has also not had a Democratic governor for more than 20 years.
Elsewhere, Democrat Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. He celebrated on stage alongside his husband in New Hampshire.
Pappas defeated former Republican Senator John Sununu in the race, whom he thanked on Tuesday, saying: "We all owe John Sununu a big debt of gratitude for his public service for the people of New Hampshire."

In Colorado, Melat Kiros became the first woman elected to Congress from Gen Z - meaning those who were born between 1997 and 2012.

articles.title_orig: CVS Health plans to split itself up. Here's why a breakup could make sense now
articles.title_zh: CVS Health plans to split itself up. Here's why a breakup could make sense now
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health plans to break itself up — and this time, the bet looks a lot more viable.
The healthcare conglomerate on Wednesday announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. CVS would separate its pharmacy business – including roughly 9,000 retail locations – from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark.
The move comes more than two years after CVS considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea. At the time, analysts questioned whether the retail pharmacy business could survive on its own.
“Back then, the idea of retail standing alone was unthinkable,” Brian Tanquilut, senior equity research analyst at Jefferies, told CNBC.
But the economics of the businesses have changed: CVS's retail pharmacy business has become more consistently profitable, while its insurer, Aetna, has improved its performance despite persistently high medical costs in Medicare Advantage plans. That could make it easier for the company to separate the units — and for investors to recognize the value of each on its own, rather than valuing them together as one sprawling healthcare conglomerate.
“For us, it's showing the stability of the pharmacy,” Michael Cherny, senior research analyst at Leerink Partners, said in an interview. “This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome.”
CVS CEO David Joyner told CNBC’s "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that back in 2024, the company was "in a turnaround" without the flexibility, cash or business performance to execute a split. Now, CVS has posted eight consecutive quarters of beating Wall Street earnings estimates and has raised its guidance several times over the last two years, thanks to improvement across its PBM, pharmacy and insurer.
Since taking the helm in 2024, Joyner has pursued an aggressive turnaround plan that involves $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.
The company also now expects to generate at least $15.5 billion in operating cash flow in 2026, a roughly 70% increase from $9.1 billion in 2024, and says it has reached its leverage target ahead of schedule.
"What's changed in two years is the fact that we now can look at this business and the assets that are assembled and really determine, without any distress or without anything that we have to do, what is the right strategic decision to make," Joyner told analysts on a call Wednesday, adding that the decision comes "out of strength."
While investors have largely cheered CVS's progress in recent years, Wall Street appeared more pessimistic about Wednesday's announcement, as the company's shares dropped about 12%.
CVS's retail business has benefited from changes in the competitive landscape, including the widespread retrenchment and store closures of Walgreens, Rite Aid and other pharmacy operators over the last few years. That’s created opportunities for CVS to gain market share, some analysts told CNBC.
CVS has also introduced changes to its pharmacy reimbursement model. Its CostVantage program is designed to replace the traditional process with a more transparent, cost-based model. Some analysts say that has helped the company better align reimbursement with the cost of dispensing prescriptions and contributed to steadier profits.
Those developments represent a meaningful shift for a business that has faced years of pressure from declining prescription reimbursement, store closures and competition from online pharmacies and other retailers.
That doesn't mean the retail pharmacy has become a high-growth business. CVS's retail pharmacy segment remains a relatively low-margin operation, with adjusted operating margins of roughly 4% to 5%. But analysts say it may now be stable and profitable enough to operate independently – even if investors value it at a discount to CVS's other businesses.
In a note Wednesday, RBC Capital Markets analyst Ben Hendrix said the lower valuation investors assign to the retail pharmacy unit has weighed on CVS's overall value and obscured the earnings strength of businesses like Aetna and Caremark.
The underlying growth of the insurance and PBM businesses is also stronger than that of retail pharmacy, Tanquilut said, after accounting for changes to Caremark's rebate arrangements.
Aetna in particular has gotten a better handle on medical costs by exiting unprofitable markets, expanding value-based care models, and tightening utilization management.
The breakup also comes as Caremark faces mounting scrutiny over PBM practices, including state-level legal and regulatory challenges involving the businesses and their relationships with pharmacies.
Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban any one company from owning both a pharmacy and a PBM — thought the Arkansas measure has been held up in court. Cherny noted that legal hurdles involving PBMs in other states have continued to pile up.
“Through what seems to be a never-ending litany of state lawsuits, it feels like it's been under more pressure,” Cherny said. “It's unclear if it just became, for lack of a better term, too tenuous to move forward with those two entities combined as one. I’m not sure.”
Even so, Joyner told the Wall Street Journal that the company wasn’t splitting up because of regulatory issues. CVS has said the separation follows a strategic review and is intended to give each business greater focus and flexibility.
The move also marks a significant departure from the integrated healthcare strategy CVS spent years building.
CVS spent roughly $70 billion to acquire Aetna in 2018 and argued that combining health insurance, pharmacy benefit management, retail pharmacies and health providers under one roof would help coordinate care and create a competitive advantage. CVS was still promoting that model as recently as its investor day last year.
The proposed split suggests the company now sees more value in separating at least some of those businesses – though it is not abandoning vertical integration altogether.
Aetna and Caremark will remain together in the healthcare company, alongside CVS’s specialty pharmacy, its primary care clinic Oak Street Health and its home-visit provider Signify Health. The separate pharmacy company will include roughly 9,000 retail stores, mail pharmacy operations and MinuteClinic, a retail medical clinic located inside certain CVS locations.
Both sides are large enough that they can stand on their own, Cherny said. Caremark is one of the country's three largest PBMs, while CVS has one of the largest retail pharmacy footprints in the U.S.
But separating the company raises questions about how much of the commercial relationship between the businesses can survive.
The relationship has historically benefited both sides. As it stands, Caremark can use CVS's extensive retail footprint to offer members convenient access to prescriptions and steer them toward CVS locations through preferred pharmacy arrangements. Programs such as Maintenance Choice, for example, give eligible members the option to fill certain maintenance medications at CVS retail pharmacies or through mail order.
Those arrangements also helped direct prescription volume to CVS's stores, giving the retail pharmacy unit an important source of customers. Because the businesses shared a parent company, the financial benefits of that relationship ultimately went to CVS as a whole.
In a note, RBC's Hendrix also raised questions about how the split could impact Aetna's Medicare Advantage quality ratings, which determine whether health plans qualify for bonus payments from the government. Retail pharmacists have played a role in engaging Aetna members, and a separation could complicate that relationship.

articles.content_orig:
Apple reportedly has a big redesign coming to next year’s iPhone Pro models, timed for the iPhone’s 20th anniversary. The latest leak about the design reveals that the dream of a cutout-free display may remain a dream for now.
Yesterday Weibo leaker Digital Chat Station outlined three new iPhone models coming in early 2027: iPhone 18e, iPhone 18, and iPhone Air 2.
His main focus was on the iPhone 18, which is expected to get two Pro-inspired upgrades .
In a follow-up post though, replying to another Weibo user’s question, the leaker addressed a key design question regarding next fall’s iPhone Pro models.
Apple is rumored to be working on a big redesign timed for the iPhone’s 20th anniversary. It will reportedly feature a quad-curved display that wraps around the edges of the device for a visually bezel-free look.
Early rumors indicated the device could also drop the Dynamic Island for a truly all-glass display, with no cutouts.
But according to Digital Chat Station, that’s not happening after all.
After being asked if the ‘iPhone 20 Pro Max’ will have a Dynamic Island still, or feature a hole-free display, the leaker confirmed the display will still have holes . Thus, it will retain the Dynamic Island cutout.
It’s unclear if the Dynamic Island will be the same size as that of iPhone 18 Pro, but since the device is expected to have Face ID, that’s highly likely.
Does the inclusion of a display cutout change your interest in the iPhone 20 Pro at all? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: From Iran to trade: how the US midterms impact the rest of the world
articles.title_zh: From Iran to trade: how the US midterms impact the rest of the world
articles.content_orig:
A display shows currency exchange information in Tehran, Iran, September 27, 2026
Photo by Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency via Reuters
By Raphael S. Cohen and Howard J. Shatz
This commentary was originally published by Foreign Policy on October 26, 2026.
So far, the Iran war has cost the United States 800 casualties, tens of billions of dollars, hundreds of damaged or destroyed buildings on U.S. military bases in the region, and a drawdown of munitions that is straining supplies. Fuel prices have risen sharply since the start of the war, pushing U.S. inflation to a level last seen in 2023. According to polls, most Americans do not believe there was “sufficient reason” for the United States to attack Iran, and public opposition to the war has increased over time. And there is little sign that the fighting is coming to a close. As of now, the Iranian regime seems disinclined to cease its attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, stop its regional proxies from attacking elsewhere, or curb its nuclear program.
What should the United States do now?
In broad strokes, there are three options. First, ramp the war back up. Some—including U.S. President Donald Trump—have floated the idea of returning to a full-scale bombing campaign similar to what we saw during the conflict's initial phase. Others have proposed escalating the war , for example by using ground forces to seize Iranian territory.
At the other end of the spectrum lies a second option: The United States could walk away from the conflict. Even Republican supporters of the Trump administration have increasingly called for an end to the war.
The third option is to stay the current course: Maintain the blockade and economic pressure campaign, respond with force when Iran or its proxies strike U.S. or partner targets, and push for negotiations that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the Iranian nuclear program. Of the three options, this may be the least satisfying; it almost certainly will not bring quick results. But it is strategically prudent.
As messy as the conflict has been, the U.S. blockade of Iran and the wider Operation Economic Outcast are going in the direction that the United States wants.
As messy as the conflict has been, the U.S. blockade of Iran and the wider Operation Economic Outcast are going in the direction that the United States wants. Iran is imploding economically. Its currency recently traded at 2.5 million rials to the dollar, a dramatic depreciation from about 630,000 to the dollar in 2024. Inflation has recently reached almost 90 percent , with food inflation at almost 130 percent. Moreover, Iran's floating oil storage—a shadow fleet of tankers anchored outside the Strait of Hormuz, whose cargo has mitigated some of the effects of the blockade—is now depleted. That further increases the pressure on the Iranian economy.
Although the U.S. spot price has risen above $100 per barrel at times, oil is still priced well below previous peaks once you adjust for inflation . Middle Eastern crude is also again flowing out of the region at near prewar levels, although other critical commodities—liquefied natural gas, refined fuels, fertilizer—remain bottlenecked.
To be fair, economic coercion—even when it causes a full economic crisis—has a mixed track record in effecting regime change. Major economic dislocations have sometimes led to dramatic changes in government, as in Yugoslavia following years of economic problems in the 1980s. Inflationary crises can facilitate democratization , as happened in much of Latin America in the 1980s. But in other cases, such as the U.S. pressure campaigns against Cuba and North Korea, the regimes were still able to use what resources they had to maintain their hold on power.
The history of the last Iran nuclear deal shows that economic pressure campaigns have a better record when they are aimed at achieving more modest objectives. In that case, mounting economic duress forced even the Iranian regime's hard-liners to the negotiating table. This time around, the regime seems even less inclined to make concessions, at least judging from its public statements, but the pressure campaign is also more extreme.
The primary downside to maintaining the current approach is that it is unlikely to lead to a swift resolution of the conflict.
The primary downside to maintaining the current approach is that it is unlikely to lead to a swift resolution of the conflict. Strategies built around economic pressure generally take months or even years to succeed. But time is on Washington's side. The blockade is continuing to bite under economic conditions that some deem “unbearable,” with unemployment rising and this year's GDP projected to shrink by 7.6 percent . If Iran can stabilize its economy, the United States will need to alter its approach. But if not, the Iranian regime—as fractured and hard-line as it may be—will sooner or later need to compromise to avoid collapse.
Moreover, the alternatives to staying the course are worse. Resuming a full-scale war to “blow the entire nation up” is unlikely to be feasible. Even if we bracket concerns over U.S. weapons stockpiles, air campaigns alone have rarely succeeded in overthrowing a government. Plus, given the intensity of the bombardment in the opening weeks of the war, it's hard to imagine what more the United States could do from the air that would tip the balance. Removing the Iranian regime by ground power would be a Herculean undertaking: Compared with Iraq, the site of the last major U.S. war in the region, Iran has nearly double the population and almost quadruple the territory.
Returning to large-scale conflict would also come at a cost. Despite the effectiveness of the bombardment from February to April, Iran still has the ability to produce missiles and drones. U.S. military casualties stand at 15 killed and more than 800 wounded , a figure that would almost certainly rise if the conflict intensified. Similarly, the war has already taken a toll on military equipment and bases in the region, and more damage would be incurred if the conflict flares up again. Then there are the less tangible costs, such as the erosion of Washington's global reputation, especially if military strikes hit civilian infrastructure.
Then there is the global economic cost of a renewed large-scale conflict. Analysts estimate that it could take years to fully repair the damage to the Middle East's energy infrastructure that has occurred so far. A return to hostilities would risk further damage to these already battered facilities, not to mention the prospect of even higher energy prices.
More modest military options also come with significant risks. The most widely discussed option is the seizure of Kharg Island , an island around 20 miles off the Iranian coast that serves as the country's hub for 90 percent of its oil exports. This would aim to either destabilize the regime or use the island as a bargaining chip in future negotiations. Although the United States certainly has the capacity to seize the island, the challenge would be holding the territory afterward. The island is well within range of Iranian missiles and drones , leaving any troops stationed there and resupply efforts vulnerable to attack. Air defenses provide only a partial solution, so the United States would likely sustain casualties. This would also create political pressure on the United States to abandon the island prematurely—before it could pressure Iran into a lasting settlement.
Walking away from the war would carry its own costs.
Walking away from the war, by contrast, carries its own costs. Iran has so far rejected proposals to allow the free passage of global exports through Hormuz in exchange for an end to the blockade. Unilaterally dropping the blockade would effectively leave the Strait of Hormuz in Iranian hands, allowing the regime to tax transiting ships as it sees fit. WASHINGTON– The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today announced approximately $967 million in additional funding through its Grid Resilience State and Tribal Formula Grant program to modernize critical energy infrastructure, lower electricity costs and strengthen America’s power grid. The funding will support locally driven projects across states, territories, and tribes to upgrade critical infrastructure, prevent power disruptions, and meet growing electricity demand while helping lower costs for American families and businesses.
The investment advances President Trump’s American energy dominance agenda and supports the priorities outlined in his Executive Order, Strengthening the Reliability and Security of the United States Electric Grid, to ensure a reliable, affordable, and secure electric grid to support American economic growth and energy security.
Projects funded through the program will help states, territories, and tribes invest in infrastructure improvements that protect against disruptive events, improve system performance, and ensure communities and businesses have dependable power when they need it most.
“Lowering costs and unleashing prosperity are top priorities for President Trump,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “These commonsense investments provide resources directly to states, territories, and tribes to lower electricity costs and strengthen grid reliability for American businesses and families.”
“A strong and dependable grid is the backbone of American economic prosperity,” said Office of Electricity Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza. “This funding will help Americans across the country, including our tribal partners, optimize their electricity systems and prepare for future growth while strengthening energy security and deploying technologies that can lower the long-term cost of delivering reliable power.”

articles.title_orig: Trump's midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data center opponents
articles.title_zh: Trump's midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data center opponents
articles.content_orig:
China, Canada, India and South Africa could gain fresh leverage in trade negotiations with Washington after Democrats seized control of both chambers of the US Congress, weakening President Donald Trump's political position amid growing discontent over the Iran war, rising consumer prices and his controversial trade tariffs.
The November 3 midterm elections saw Republicans lose their majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, with Democrats securing victories in Republican strongholds, including Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.
Republicans suffered the setback amid rising living costs, Trump's tariffs and the eight-month Iran war, which disrupted energy supplies and pushed Brent crude to $138.21 per barrel in April, its highest level since 2008, fuelling US inflation.
From what Business Insider Africa has gathered, the results could encourage America's trade rivals and dissatisfied partners to resist Washington's demands, delay investments and seek better trade deals as Trump will now have to answer to a Democrat-controlled Congress.
DON'T MISS: Despite warnings from China, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, Israel presses ahead with embassy plans in breakaway African territory near Red Sea
China is among the countries that could use Trump's weakened political position to push for more favourable trade terms, particularly as Beijing seeks to recover exports lost to American tariffs.
The impact of those restrictions is reflected in US trade figures, which show that America's goods trade deficit with China narrowed from $295.5 billion in 2024 to $202.1 billion in 2025.
With a temporary trade truce approaching expiration in January 2027, Beijing could seek lower tariffs and fewer technology restrictions, calculating that Trump faces greater political resistance to another trade war.
Saul Eslake, an economist at Corinna Economic Advisory in Australia, believes China could take advantage of the changing political balance in Washington.
"Xi Jinping will recognize that Trump's authority has been greatly weakened by these results, and will no doubt be thinking about ways of exploiting that," Eslake told Reuters.
Although Beijing has not publicly indicated plans to exploit Trump's political setback, China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning described the elections as an internal US matter, saying the country would continue managing differences and expanding cooperation with Washington.

Canada could also find greater support in Washington after months of difficult trade negotiations between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Trump's administration over tariffs and market access.
Talks stalled in August after Ottawa rejected American demands, while tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium and other products continued to strain relations between the neighbouring economies.
In an October 30 interview with POLITICO, Carney indicated that Canada would rather wait for another American president than accept an unfavourable agreement.
Asked whether Canada could hold out until Trump's successor took office, he replied: "Well, if that's what it takes, yeah."
His position could receive support from Democrats, particularly Senator Ron Wyden, a senior member of the Senate Finance Committee, who has called for removing tariffs on Canadian goods because of their impact on businesses and consumers.
DON'T MISS: European nation stops foreign workers and students from South Africa, Ghana, India and other countries from applying for residence permits inside the country
India could gain negotiating flexibility as New Delhi seeks better trade terms while American consumers face higher prices on imported goods.
Washington imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Indian products in 2025 amid trade disputes and disagreements over India's purchases of Russian oil. The restrictions affected textiles, jewellery and footwear, increasing costs for American importers.
The countries agreed in February 2026 to a framework reducing tariffs on most Indian goods to 18%, but negotiations remain unfinished.
Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the agreement had reached the final drafting stage, although New Delhi would proceed only if it secured an advantage over competing exporters.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman also acknowledged in October that further concessions would be "very, very difficult" for both sides.
The Democratic victory could encourage India to resist additional demands as Trump faces greater scrutiny of his trade policies from the Democrat-controlled Congress.
South Africa faces a trade setback after Washington announced on November 2 that it would remove the country from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) on January 1, 2027, following months of diplomatic tensions over Pretoria's domestic and foreign policies.
The decision threatens preferential access for South African exports, including vehicles, citrus fruits and wine, adding to existing trade pressures after the country's agricultural exports to the US fell by 28% in the second quarter of 2026.
President Cyril Ramaphosa previously urged South Africans to prepare for possible exclusion, saying: "We should not go out and jump off tall buildings and think that this is the end of the world."
However, in a sharp reversal of his earlier cautious stance, Ramaphosa welcomed the Democratic victory on November 4, saying: "We have seen that the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken."
He added that the results could introduce "a new era in world relations", raising hopes of improved ties with Washington.
"We're hoping that, on a bilateral basis, there will be a coming together of minds, where we will find a proper path forward on geopolitics as well as on trade matters and investment matters," Ramaphosa said.

articles.title_orig: UK Supreme Court hears appeal against Palestine Action’s proscription
articles.title_zh: UK Supreme Court hears appeal against Palestine Action’s proscription
articles.content_orig:
An appeal challenging the designation of Palestine Action as a “terrorist” organisation has begun at the United Kingdom’s top court, as police arrested demonstrators who gathered outside to protest against the group’s proscription.
The two-day hearing at the Supreme Court in London began on Wednesday. Huda Ammori, cofounder of Palestine Action, said ahead of the hearing that she would argue the ban is having a disproportionate effect on freedom of speech and the right to protest.
The direct action group was proscribed by the UK government under then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer in July last year. The decision has since been denounced by rights groups, including Amnesty International and Liberty.
Palestine Action describes itself as a “direct action movement committed to ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime”. Its designation as a “terrorist” organisation puts it on the same list as armed groups such as al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS). Those found guilty of belonging to or supporting Palestine Action could face up to 14 years in prison.
As the hearing got under way, protesters gathered outside the court. Some expressed support for Palestine Action, while others opposed the group’s proscription, which many view as an affront to civil liberties. One demonstrator held a placard reading: “God help us Jews who support Palestine and Palestine Action”.
About 25 protesters were arrested, according to the Press Association; the final person detained carried a sign saying: “God help us who are not married to the UK’s national security adviser who support Palestine and Palestine action.”
It’s understood that this is in reference to journalist and author Sarah Helm, who is married to the UK prime minister’s national security adviser, and who had earlier posted a similar line on X but did not face prosecution.
In a statement issued after the first day of the hearing, Ammori said that “overwhelming evidence” given to the court by United Nations experts, Amnesty International, Liberty and the former director of MI6 showed that the “dangerous and disproportionate proscription” had criminalised legitimate protest as “terrorism” for the “first time in British history”.
She said the government’s submissions were “particularly lacklustre”.
Ammori said the government was “clearly struggling with the consequences of this ban”.
Ammori said Palestine Action “has never advocated violence against any person”, and that it used tactics including “graffiti, petty vandalism, occupation and lock-ons”.
More than 4,000 people had been arrested for peacefully opposing Israel’s war on Gaza, she noted.
“This ban has made Britain an international aberration on free speech.” Ammori urged the justices “to bring this authoritarian overreach… to an end once and for all”.
“Today was another demonstration of the chaos wrought by the Government’s grave misuse of terrorism powers to proscribe Palestine Action,” Tom Southerden, Amnesty International’s UK Law and Human Rights director, said in a statement issued after Wednesday’s arrests.
“The sight of musicians, politicians and celebrities being arrested for peacefully holding placards is a grim one. That they were arrested for using the same language that Sarah Helm didn’t face arrest for, shows how dangerously vague our terrorism laws are.”
Amnesty is one of several organisations calling for the UK government to lift the ban on Palestine Action.
“Whatever the Supreme Court ultimately decides, it’s long past time for the Government to admit they got this badly wrong, end the proscription of Palestine Action and put a stop to these appalling arrests,” Southerden said.
The UK government’s crackdown on pro-Palestine voices has come under intense scrutiny since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza more than three years ago.
Last week, Swedish academic Andreas Malm was prevented from entering the UK after the government said his presence was “not conducive to the public good”. Malm is a vocal supporter of Palestine and has spoken out against Israel’s assault on Gaza.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said before taking office in July that the Labour Party had “got it wrong” on Gaza. However, his comments have come under renewed scrutiny after Malm was refused entry to the UK last week.

articles.title_orig: Mark Zuckerberg Passes Michael Dell To Become Fifth-Richest As Meta Rallies After Midterms
articles.title_zh: Mark Zuckerberg Passes Michael Dell To Become Fifth-Richest As Meta Rallies After Midterms
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Meta’s Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has wielded enormous power over the social media empire he built more than two decades ago, leading the California juggernaut through major scandals, scrutiny and technological shifts.
But the 42-year-old tech mogul considered leaving the state because he feared that a ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of California billionaires could reduce the amount of control he has over Meta, a recent regulatory filing shows. Meta’s board struck a deal so he would stay in California. Meta is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
The filing highlights how one of the world’s wealthiest people, whose net worth totals more than $200 billion, is bracing for the possibility that California voters pass Proposition 40, a wealth tax proposal that would primarily be used to fund healthcare.
Although supporters say the fear that billionaires will flee the state are overblown, the ultrawealthy have made moves to potentially avoid paying the tax or are funding campaigns to defeat it.
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Zuckerberg’s influence over Meta is partly tied to how the company structures its stock. Zuckerberg holds roughly 60% of voting power over Meta even though he only owns about 13% of the company’s total shares.
Meta has a dual-class share structure, dividing the stock into Class A shares with one vote each and Class B shares with 10 votes each. Zuckerberg holds a large amount of Class B stock, which gives him majority control over company decisions.
If the wealth tax proposal passes, Zuckerberg is worried that it could reduce his voting power, according to the filing. The tech executive makes an annual salary of $1, so most of his wealth is linked to his stake in Meta. If he had to sell his Class B shares to pay the tax, that would reduce his voting majority in the company, according to the filing.
In September, he told Meta’s board that he planned to list his Palo Alto home for sale, pressuring board members to find a solution.
On Wednesday, Meta announced a new class of stock with no voting rights called Class C that would take effect in January. As part of the deal, Zuckerberg could sell or transfer up to 20% of Class C stock so his voting majority doesn’t decrease even if he has to pay the tax.
“Mr. Zuckerberg’s continued leadership role in our Company, and his continuing presence at the Company’s headquarters in California, is critical at this current inflection point for the Company and the tech industry in order to continue to provide value-maximization for all shareholders,” the filing said.
Since the company’s public debut, its share price has risen more than 1,700%, outperforming the S&P 500.
In Meta’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said creating a new class of nonvoting stock benefits the company in various ways, including “capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, other general corporate purposes.”
“We believe this share class will maintain our founder-led structure. It will expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI,” she said.
Meta has roughly 66,700 workers globally. Its sprawling headquarters is in Menlo Park.
Some billionaires such as Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey, Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen and Google co-founder Sergey Brin have opposed the wealth tax proposal. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, on the other hand, has said he doesn’t mind paying more taxes.
The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West is backing the wealth tax proposal and says it applies to roughly 200 billionaires who have resided in California as of January 1, 2026, and could raise $100 billion.
More than $300 million has been contributed to fight the billionaire tax, including two propositions that could block it if they gather more votes. Although stock prices fluctuate, Zuckerberg could face a tax liability of roughly $12 billion based on his net worth.
In 2015, Zuckerberg and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan, pledged to give away 99% of his Facebook shares over their lifetimes when they celebrated the birth of their first daughter.
The couple created the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, a philanthropic organization whose efforts include curing, managing and preventing all diseases. Although Zuckerberg lives in Palo Alto, he also owns real estate elsewhere, including in Hawaii, Washington, D.C. and Ireland.
Times data journalist Gabrielle LaMarr LeMee contributed to this report.
